questions.title: Streaming Bronze Ingestion with Auto Loader and Schema Evolution
questions.prompt: Your team ingests JSON event files that land continuously in an ADLS Gen2 container into a Bronze Delta table using Databricks Auto Loader. Write the PySpark streaming read-and-write code that uses cloudFiles to ingest the JSON files incrementally, with schema inference and schema evolution enabled, writing out to a managed Bronze Delta table. Then explain exactly what happens the very first time an upstream producer adds a brand-new field to the JSON payload, and separately what happens if an existing field's data type changes (for example, a field that used to arrive as an integer starts arriving as a string).
questions.modelAnswer:
Auto Loader is configured through the cloudFiles source: format("cloudFiles") with cloudFiles.format set to the raw file type (json here), a cloudFiles.schemaLocation where Auto Loader persists the schema it has inferred so far across restarts, and cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode to control how new fields are handled. On the write side, the streaming query targets a Delta table with checkpointLocation for exactly-once restart semantics and mergeSchema enabled so new columns Auto Loader detects are allowed to flow into the target table's schema rather than being rejected.

The first time an upstream producer adds a brand-new field, Auto Loader's default schema evolution mode (addNewColumns) deliberately fails the current micro-batch with an UnknownFieldException. That failure isn't a bug to work around -- it's the mechanism: Auto Loader updates the persisted schema in the schema location to include the new column, and the stream needs to be restarted (Databricks Jobs with automatic retries handle this transparently) to pick up the new schema. On restart, the new field flows through normally and, because mergeSchema is set on the Delta write, gets added to the Bronze table as a new column (existing rows simply show it as NULL retroactively). If you instead set cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode to "rescue", the stream never fails at all -- unrecognized new columns get captured in a _rescued_data column (a JSON-encoded catch-all) instead of triggering a restart, trading immediate visibility for continuous uptime.

A field changing type is a different failure mode entirely, because Auto Loader does not retroactively widen or change an already-inferred column's type. When incoming data no longer matches the inferred type for a column (an integer field suddenly receiving string values), with the rescued data column enabled (which it is by default when schema inference is used) the mismatched value for that row gets diverted into _rescued_data rather than crashing the pipeline or silently corrupting the typed column -- the typed column itself gets NULL for that row. This is exactly why Bronze layer design treats _rescued_data as a required, monitored column: it's where every type-mismatch casualty ends up, and a growing _rescued_data payload is the signal that an upstream contract has silently drifted and needs a deliberate schema fix, not just reinference.
questions.professionalAnswer:
When I set up Auto Loader for a Bronze layer, I always point cloudFiles.schemaLocation at a durable path so the inferred schema survives restarts, and I leave the evolution mode on its default, addNewColumns, because I want to know when the shape of the data changes rather than have it happen silently. So the first time a new field shows up, the stream deliberately fails -- that's not Auto Loader breaking, that's Auto Loader telling me the schema just changed. It's already updated the schema file by the time it throws, so all I have to do is restart the stream and the new column shows up in the Bronze table because I've got mergeSchema turned on for the Delta write.

A type change is a completely different animal, and I make sure people on my team don't conflate the two. Auto Loader isn't going to retroactively decide a column that's always been an integer should now be a string -- instead, any row where the incoming value doesn't match what was inferred gets siphoned off into the _rescued_data column, and the real typed column just gets a null for that row. I treat _rescued_data as a load-bearing part of every Bronze table, not an edge case -- if I see it start filling up, that's my signal that some upstream system changed a field's type or shape without telling anyone, and I need to go fix the contract rather than just let the inference quietly keep eating the mismatches.
questions.example:
from pyspark.sql.functions import current_timestamp

bronze_df = (
    spark.readStream
        .format("cloudFiles")
        .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
        .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/mnt/checkpoints/bronze_events/_schema")
        .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns")
        .option("cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes", "true")
        .load("/mnt/raw/events/")
        .withColumn("_ingested_at", current_timestamp())
)

(
    bronze_df.writeStream
        .format("delta")
        .option("checkpointLocation", "/mnt/checkpoints/bronze_events/_checkpoint")
        .option("mergeSchema", "true")
        .trigger(availableNow=True)
        .toTable("bronze.events")
)
commonMistakes: Not setting a durable cloudFiles.schemaLocation, so the inferred schema is lost and re-inferred (possibly differently) on every restart
Omitting mergeSchema on the Delta write, so a newly-detected column gets rejected by the target table even after Auto Loader itself has already evolved its schema
Treating the UnknownFieldException on a new field as a pipeline bug to silence rather than the intended restart signal
Assuming a type change (e.g. int to string) gets coerced or merged the same way a brand-new column does
Ignoring the _rescued_data column instead of monitoring it as the early-warning signal for upstream schema drift
keyPoints: cloudFiles.schemaLocation persists the inferred schema across stream restarts
Default schema evolution mode (addNewColumns) deliberately fails the batch once when a new field appears, then restarts cleanly
mergeSchema on the Delta writeStream is required for the new column to actually land in the target table
A type change does not evolve the column's type; mismatched values are diverted into _rescued_data instead
_rescued_data should be monitored, not ignored -- it's where type-mismatch casualties accumulate
schemaEvolutionMode: "rescue" avoids the restart-on-new-field behavior entirely, at the cost of immediate visibility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Auto Loader cloudFiles streaming read configuration
Correct Delta writeStream with checkpoint and mergeSchema
Accurately explains the addNewColumns fail-then-restart behavior for a new field
Accurately explains that a type change routes to _rescued_data rather than evolving the column
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Upserting Changed Customers with MERGE INTO, Then Z-Ordering for Lookups
questions.prompt: A nightly CDC batch lands in a staging Delta table staging.customer_changes containing customer_id plus the latest attribute values for customers that are new or have changed since the last run. Write a Delta Lake MERGE INTO statement that upserts those changes into curated.customers: insert customers that don't yet exist, update attributes on customers that actually changed, and do nothing for customers that landed in staging unchanged. Then explain why you'd follow this merge with an OPTIMIZE curated.customers ZORDER BY (customer_id) command, and what Z-ordering is actually doing on disk that makes it worth running.
questions.modelAnswer:
The MERGE joins staging.customer_changes to curated.customers on customer_id. The WHEN NOT MATCHED branch handles brand-new customers with a plain INSERT. The WHEN MATCHED branch is where the 'do nothing for unchanged rows' requirement actually gets enforced: without a change-detection predicate, MERGE would blindly UPDATE every matched row every night even when nothing actually changed, which is wasted write amplification against a Delta table. Adding a predicate like (tgt.email IS DISTINCT FROM src.email OR tgt.phone IS DISTINCT FROM src.phone OR ...) to the WHEN MATCHED clause means the UPDATE only fires for rows where at least one tracked attribute genuinely differs; rows where nothing changed simply don't match any WHEN clause and are left completely untouched. IS DISTINCT FROM is the deliberate choice over <> or !=, because standard inequality comparisons involving NULL evaluate to NULL (neither true nor false) rather than true, so a column that goes from a real value to NULL (or vice versa) would silently fail to trigger an update with <> -- IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as a comparable value and correctly flags that as a change.

OPTIMIZE curated.customers ZORDER BY (customer_id) is worth running afterward for two separate reasons stacked together. First, OPTIMIZE performs file compaction (bin-packing): every MERGE, even one that only touches a handful of rows, can leave behind small files from the rewritten data files, and a table accumulating many small files forces downstream readers to open, read metadata from, and close far more files than necessary. OPTIMIZE rewrites those into fewer, larger files close to Delta's target file size. Second, and this is what ZORDER BY specifically adds on top of plain compaction: Delta tracks min/max statistics per file for data skipping, and Z-ordering physically co-locates rows with similar values of the Z-order column(s) into the same files during that rewrite. For a table like curated.customers that gets queried and joined constantly on customer_id, that co-location means each file's min/max range for customer_id becomes narrow and distinctive instead of overlapping broadly with every other file -- so a query filtering or joining on a specific customer_id can skip reading the vast majority of files entirely, because Delta can prove from the file-level statistics alone that the value can't be in them.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I always write this kind of MERGE with the no-op case in mind first, because that's the part people forget. The ON clause joins on customer_id, WHEN NOT MATCHED just inserts the new customer -- that part's easy. The WHEN MATCHED clause is where I add a change-detection condition across the attributes I actually care about, and I specifically use IS DISTINCT FROM instead of a plain not-equal, because not-equal against NULL in SQL just evaluates to unknown, not true -- so if a customer's phone number goes from having a value to NULL, a plain <> comparison would quietly never flag that as a change. IS DISTINCT FROM is the null-safe version that actually catches it. With that predicate in place, rows that genuinely didn't change don't match any WHEN clause at all, so MERGE leaves them alone -- which is exactly the 'do nothing' behavior being asked for.

As for OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY afterward -- I think of that as two favors in one command. OPTIMIZE alone just compacts the small files that a nightly MERGE tends to leave scattered around into fewer, bigger ones, which cuts down on file-open overhead for anyone reading the table. ZORDER BY customer_id is the extra step that actually sorts and co-locates data by that column while it's doing the rewrite, so each resulting file ends up covering a narrow, distinct range of customer_id values instead of a little bit of everything. That matters because Delta keeps min/max stats per file, and a query or join hitting a specific customer_id can use those narrow ranges to skip almost every file in the table instead of scanning all of them.
questions.example:
MERGE INTO curated.customers AS tgt
USING staging.customer_changes AS src
ON tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED AND (
       tgt.email        IS DISTINCT FROM src.email
    OR tgt.phone         IS DISTINCT FROM src.phone
    OR tgt.address_line1 IS DISTINCT FROM src.address_line1
    OR tgt.loyalty_tier   IS DISTINCT FROM src.loyalty_tier
) THEN UPDATE SET
    tgt.email         = src.email,
    tgt.phone          = src.phone,
    tgt.address_line1  = src.address_line1,
    tgt.loyalty_tier    = src.loyalty_tier,
    tgt.updated_at      = current_timestamp()
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (
    customer_id, email, phone, address_line1, loyalty_tier, updated_at
) VALUES (
    src.customer_id, src.email, src.phone, src.address_line1, src.loyalty_tier, current_timestamp()
);

OPTIMIZE curated.customers
ZORDER BY (customer_id);
commonMistakes: Using <> or != instead of IS DISTINCT FROM, silently missing changes that involve NULL
Omitting a change-detection predicate entirely, causing every matched row to be rewritten on every run
Forgetting the WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT branch, so brand-new customers never make it into the curated table
Running OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY on a very large table far more often than the write pattern justifies, burning unnecessary compute
Choosing a ZORDER column that doesn't match the table's actual filter/join predicates, gaining no data-skipping benefit
keyPoints: ON clause joins on the natural/primary key (customer_id)
WHEN MATCHED uses a null-safe change predicate (IS DISTINCT FROM) so unchanged rows are true no-ops
WHEN NOT MATCHED handles inserts for brand-new customers
OPTIMIZE compacts small files left behind by incremental merges
ZORDER BY co-locates rows by the given column(s) so file-level min/max statistics enable data skipping
ZORDER columns should match real, frequent query/join predicates to pay off

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct overall MERGE INTO structure
Correct null-safe no-op/change-detection predicate on WHEN MATCHED
Correct WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT clause
Explains OPTIMIZE's file-compaction purpose
Explains Z-ordering's data-skipping mechanism via file statistics
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Rolling 5-Minute Event Counts per Device with summarize and bin()
questions.prompt: Telemetry events are landing in an Eventhouse table named DeviceEvents with columns Timestamp (datetime), DeviceId (string), and EventType (string). Write a KQL query that returns, for each device, the count of events in each 5-minute bucket over the last 24 hours. Then explain why bin() is the right tool for this bucketing versus truncating the timestamp with string manipulation or a manual floor-division group-by, and what you'd need to change if the business instead wanted each bucket to align to the start of the local business day in a non-UTC time zone rather than bin()'s default UTC-epoch-relative boundaries.
questions.modelAnswer:
bin() rounds a value down to the nearest multiple of a given step, computed relative to a fixed origin -- for datetime values, effectively an epoch-relative floor operation, not a floor relative to the start of whatever day or hour happens to contain the value. Used as a grouping key inside summarize, bin(Timestamp, 5m) produces a true datetime value, one per five-minute bucket, and summarize count() by DeviceId, Bucket then does exactly what's being asked: one row per device per five-minute window, with a real aggregate count.

That's a categorically better approach than truncating the timestamp as a string (formatting it down to the minute and slicing off the trailing digits) or hand-rolling a floor-division against the Unix epoch. A string-truncated bucket loses the datetime type entirely -- you can no longer sort it chronologically, filter it with datetime comparisons, or join it against another time-bucketed series without reparsing it back into a datetime first. A manual floor-division is just reimplementing what bin() already does natively, except error-prone and unreadable, and it doesn't get the query engine's native optimizations for a well-known scalar function. bin() is also the one documented, idiomatic way every other KQL time-series operator (like make-series) expects bucketing to be expressed, so using it keeps the query composable with the rest of Kusto's time-series surface.

bin()'s bucket boundaries are anchored to an implicit origin that is effectively UTC, not to any particular timezone's calendar day. For a 5-minute bucket size that divides evenly into 60, this happens to line up with clock-minute boundaries in any timezone, but it will never shift to align with, say, the start of a business day that begins at a non-midnight-UTC local hour. To anchor buckets to a specific reference point instead of the implicit UTC origin, you switch from bin() to bin_at(value, bin_size, reference), supplying an explicit reference datetime (the start of that local business day, computed and adjusted for the target UTC offset). Every bucket produced is then offset from that supplied reference instead of from bin()'s default origin.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first instinct for 'count events per device in rolling five-minute buckets' is summarize count() by DeviceId and bin(Timestamp, 5m) -- bin() rounds a datetime down to the nearest five-minute mark, and because it returns a real datetime, I can sort, filter, or join on that bucket just like any other timestamp column. I'd explain to someone why I wouldn't instead chop the timestamp into a string and group on that: the second you truncate to a string, you've thrown away the type -- no more chronological ordering, no more datetime math, and you're stuck re-parsing it the moment you need to do anything else with it. Same complaint with hand-rolling a floor-division yourself -- you're just badly reinventing a function Kusto already gives you for free, and for no benefit.

Where it gets more interesting is when someone wants the buckets to align to something other than Kusto's default. bin() measures its buckets from an implicit UTC-based origin, so for something like a five-minute window that happens to line up with every clock's minute marks anyway -- but if the ask is 'align to the start of our local business day,' which almost certainly isn't UTC midnight, bin() alone can't do that; it has no concept of your business's calendar. That's what bin_at() is for -- same idea as bin(), except you hand it an explicit reference datetime to measure every bucket from, so you compute the local business day's start as a datetime and that becomes the new anchor instead of Kusto's default origin.
questions.example:
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| summarize EventCount = count() by DeviceId, Bucket = bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| order by DeviceId asc, Bucket asc

// Anchored to a custom reference (e.g. local business-day start) instead of
// bin()'s default UTC-epoch-relative origin:
let localDayStart = datetime(2026-10-09T05:00:00Z); // business day start, adjusted for local UTC offset
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| summarize EventCount = count() by DeviceId, Bucket = bin_at(Timestamp, 5m, localDayStart)
| order by DeviceId asc, Bucket asc
commonMistakes: Grouping by a string-truncated timestamp instead of bin(), losing datetime type and sortability
Hand-rolling a floor-division bucket instead of using the native bin() function
Assuming bin() automatically respects a local timezone when its boundaries are actually UTC/epoch-relative
Forgetting the ago(24h) time filter, scanning the entire table unnecessarily
Confusing bin() with bin_at() and not realizing only the latter accepts an explicit reference point
keyPoints: bin() produces a real datetime grouping key usable directly inside summarize
summarize count() by DeviceId, bin(Timestamp, 5m) yields one row per device per 5-minute bucket
bin() is preferred over string truncation or manual floor-division because it preserves the datetime type and composability
bin()'s boundaries are relative to an implicit UTC/epoch-based origin, not any particular calendar day
bin_at(value, size, reference) is the tool for anchoring buckets to an explicit reference point (e.g. a local business day start)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct summarize + bin() query with device/time grouping
Correct time-range filter (ago(24h))
Explains why bin() beats string truncation or manual floor-division
Correctly explains bin()'s default UTC-epoch-relative boundary behavior
Correctly introduces bin_at() with an explicit reference for custom alignment

questions.title: Tumbling-Window Averages in a Fabric Eventstream Before Writing to a KQL Database
questions.prompt: Sensor readings are flowing into a Fabric Eventstream from an IoT source, with each event carrying DeviceId, Temperature, and an EventTime field. Define the Eventstream transformation, expressed as the equivalent query/configuration you'd set up, that applies a 1-minute tumbling window to compute the average temperature per device before routing the aggregated output to a KQL database for downstream querying. Then explain what happens to an event that arrives late, after the 1-minute window it belongs to has already closed and emitted its aggregate, and how you'd configure the Eventstream to control that behavior.
questions.modelAnswer:
A tumbling window is fixed-size, non-overlapping, and contiguous: every event belongs to exactly one window, determined by its event-time field (EventTime here, not the time it happened to arrive at the stream). In the Eventstream's Group by / aggregate transformation, that means setting EventTime as the designated event-time column, grouping by DeviceId, applying a 1-minute tumbling window, and computing AVG(Temperature) as the aggregate -- producing one row per device per minute once each window closes.

A window can't literally wait forever for every possible straggler event before deciding it's 'done' and emitting its aggregate, so the engine relies on a watermark: effectively the maximum event time seen so far, minus a configured late-arrival/out-of-order tolerance. Once the watermark advances past a window's end boundary, that window is considered closed and its aggregate is emitted downstream to the KQL database. An event that arrives after its window has already closed and emitted does not get retroactively folded into that aggregate -- Eventstream doesn't go back and revise a result it's already sent downstream. By default, that late event is simply dropped from the aggregation; it contributes to no average at all unless the stream's tolerance window was wide enough to still cover it when the window closed.

To control this, you tune the Eventstream's late-arrival (out-of-order events) tolerance setting: widening it holds each window open longer before committing to a watermark advance, giving slower-arriving events a real chance to be included at the cost of added end-to-end latency on every window's output. It's a direct trade-off between completeness and freshness, and it should be set based on how late events in that specific source realistically arrive, not left at a default that either drops meaningful data or delays every aggregate unnecessarily. For visibility into what's being lost, you can also route events that still exceed even the widened tolerance to an error/dead-letter output rather than letting them vanish silently.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I think about a tumbling window as a strict partition of time: every event lands in exactly one non-overlapping bucket based on its own event-time field, never based on when the stream happened to receive it. So setting this up in Eventstream, I make sure EventTime is the column driving the windowing (not ingestion time), group by DeviceId, pick a 1-minute tumbling window, and aggregate with an average on Temperature -- one row per device, per minute, once each window finally closes.

The part people usually get wrong is assuming a late event just quietly gets added to whatever aggregate it was supposed to belong to. It doesn't -- once a window's watermark has advanced past it and the aggregate's already been emitted downstream, that result is final. Eventstream isn't going to reopen it. So a straggler that shows up after that point is simply dropped from the computation, full stop, unless I'd configured enough late-arrival tolerance to still cover it when the window closed. That tolerance setting is really the only lever here: widen it and I accept more delay on every window's output in exchange for catching more of the late data; tighten it and results come out faster but I drop more stragglers. I'd also usually want a dead-letter path for anything that misses even the widened tolerance, just so 'how much are we actually losing' is something I can see rather than something that silently happens.
questions.example:
-- Equivalent streaming aggregation logic for the Eventstream's
-- Group by / tumbling window transformation node:
SELECT
    DeviceId,
    AVG(Temperature) AS AvgTemperature,
    System.Timestamp() AS WindowEndTime
INTO
    [KqlDatabaseOutput]
FROM
    [IotEventstreamInput] TIMESTAMP BY EventTime
GROUP BY
    DeviceId,
    TumblingWindow(minute, 1)

-- Eventstream settings to configure (Eventstream > Settings):
--   Timestamp column:            EventTime
--   Out-of-order / late arrival tolerance: e.g. 30 seconds
--   Error output (optional):     route events exceeding tolerance to a dead-letter stream
commonMistakes: Not designating EventTime as the event-time column, so windowing falls back to arrival/ingestion time
Assuming a late event gets retroactively merged into an already-emitted window's aggregate
Setting the late-arrival tolerance far higher than necessary, adding unacceptable latency to every window's output
Grouping by DeviceId without the tumbling window, producing one ever-growing running aggregate instead of per-window results
Not configuring a dead-letter/error output, losing visibility into how much late data is being silently dropped
keyPoints: Tumbling windows are fixed-size, non-overlapping, and based on event time, not arrival time
The transformation needs an explicit event-time column, a device grouping, a window duration, and an aggregate
Windows close based on a watermark: max event time seen minus the configured late-arrival tolerance
An event arriving after its window has closed and emitted is dropped, not merged in retroactively
Late-arrival tolerance is a direct trade-off between completeness and latency
A dead-letter/error output gives visibility into events dropped beyond tolerance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct tumbling window aggregation definition (grouping, window duration, aggregate)
Correctly identifies EventTime as the required event-time column
Explains watermark-based window closing
Correctly explains that a late event is dropped, not retroactively merged

Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: A Reusable Terraform Module for Fabric Capacity and Event Hub, Called Per Environment
questions.prompt: Write a Terraform module (variables, resource block(s), outputs) that provisions a Microsoft Fabric capacity and an Event Hub namespace as reusable, parameterized infrastructure -- capacity SKU, Event Hub namespace SKU/throughput units, and resource naming should all come from input variables, never be hardcoded in the resource blocks. Then explain how you'd structure the root module to call this module twice, once for dev and once for prod, with different variable values, without duplicating the resource definitions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Every environment-specific value -- the SKU for the Fabric capacity, the Event Hub namespace's SKU and throughput units, and anything that feeds into resource names -- is declared as a module input variable, with the resource blocks themselves referencing only var.* and never a literal. That's what makes the module reusable rather than a copy-paste template: the module's logic (what resource types get created and how they're wired together) is fixed and lives in one place, while every difference between environments is pushed up into variable values supplied by the caller.

To use that module for both dev and prod without duplicating the resource definitions, the root module (or a per-environment root, depending on how state is organized) declares two separate module blocks pointing at the same source path -- the identical module code -- but passes different variable values into each: smaller SKU and fewer throughput units for dev, larger for prod, and environment-qualified names so the globally-unique Event Hub namespace name doesn't collide between the two. Terraform treats each module block as creating its own fully independent set of resource instances, addressable in state as module.dev.azurerm_fabric_capacity.this and module.prod.azurerm_fabric_capacity.this respectively -- there's no shared resource, no risk of one environment's apply touching the other's resources, as long as each environment also gets its own state (either via separate state files/backends per environment, or Terraform workspaces, or simply separate root module directories each calling the shared child module with a dev.tfvars / prod.tfvars file). The module's source code is written and reviewed exactly once; environments differ only in the variable values fed into otherwise identical module calls.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I structure this, nothing environment-specific ever gets typed directly into the resource blocks -- SKU, throughput units, even the naming all come in as variables, so the module itself is just the shape of the infrastructure, not any particular environment's infrastructure. That's the whole point of pulling it out into its own module directory in the first place.

Then at the root level, I just call that module twice -- module "dev" and module "prod", both pointing at the exact same source path, so I'm never maintaining two copies of the resource logic. All that changes between the two blocks is the variable values I hand each one: a small SKU and low throughput for dev, a bigger one for prod, and I make sure the naming variable bakes in the environment so the Event Hub namespace name -- which has to be globally unique -- doesn't collide between the two. Terraform treats those as two completely separate sets of resources under the hood, tracked separately in state under module.dev.* and module.prod.*, so an apply against one can't accidentally touch the other, especially if I also keep each environment's state isolated rather than cramming both into one shared state file.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding SKU or naming values inside the module's resource blocks instead of exposing them as variables
Forgetting that Event Hub namespace names must be globally unique, causing a collision if dev/prod names aren't distinguished
Copy-pasting the entire module directory for a second environment instead of calling the same module twice with different variables
Marking the connection string output as a plain (non-sensitive) output, leaking it into state output and logs
Sharing a single state/backend across dev and prod module calls, risking one environment's apply affecting the other
keyPoints: All environment-specific values are variables; no literals in the module's resource blocks
The same module source, called multiple times with different variable values, creates fully independent resource instances
Each module call is independently addressable in state (module.dev.*, module.prod.*)
Naming variables must guarantee global uniqueness for namespaced Azure resources like Event Hub
Sensitive outputs (connection strings) must be marked sensitive
Environments should also have isolated state, not just isolated variable values

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct variables exposing SKU, naming, and throughput inputs
Correct resource blocks fully parameterized with no hardcoded values
Correct outputs, including sensitive marking on the connection string
Explains calling the module twice with different variable values without duplicating resource code
Addresses state isolation and naming-uniqueness between environments

questions.title: Deploying Azure SQL with Bicep, and What a Missing Default Parameter Does in CI/CD
questions.prompt: Write a Bicep template that deploys an Azure SQL logical server, a database on that server, and a firewall rule allowing Azure services to connect, using parameters for the server name, admin login, admin password, database SKU, and the firewall rule's IP range. Then explain the real difference between a Bicep parameter declared with a default value and one declared without a default, specifically in terms of what happens when that template is deployed non-interactively from a CI/CD pipeline.
questions.modelAnswer:
A Bicep parameter declared with a default value is optional at deployment time: if the caller, whether that's a CI/CD pipeline, an az deployment command, or another module, doesn't explicitly supply a value, Bicep silently falls back to the default and the deployment proceeds without complaint. A parameter declared without a default is required: Bicep/ARM validates that every required parameter has a supplied value before the deployment is even allowed to start, and if one is missing, the deployment fails immediately at validation with an explicit 'missing required parameter' error.

That distinction matters most for a non-interactive CI/CD pipeline, because there's no human sitting at a prompt to supply a forgotten value -- whatever behavior the parameter declaration specifies is exactly what happens, with zero chance for someone to notice and type in a correction partway through. For a value like location or databaseSku, where there's a sensible standard choice most deployments should use, a default is appropriate: it lets most pipeline runs omit it entirely while still allowing an override when a specific deployment genuinely needs one. For sqlAdminLogin and especially sqlAdminPassword, the opposite is true: those should be required parameters with no default (the password additionally marked @secure() so it's never persisted in deployment history or logs), precisely because you want a hard, explicit failure forcing the pipeline to pull the value from a key vault or secure variable group every single time, rather than risk a template silently deploying with some hardcoded or forgotten placeholder credential baked into source control.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd put it: a default value makes a parameter optional, no default makes it mandatory, and the difference only really bites once nobody's around to catch a mistake -- which is exactly the situation in a CI/CD pipeline. If a parameter has a default and the pipeline doesn't pass anything for it, the deployment just quietly uses that default and keeps going. If there's no default and the pipeline forgets to pass it, the deployment refuses to even start -- it fails validation up front with a clear error instead of limping along with some guessed value.

That's why I'm deliberate about which of my parameters get defaults. Something like location or the database SKU, where there's a perfectly reasonable standard choice -- sure, give it a default, so most runs don't even have to think about it but can still override it when they need to. But the admin login and especially the admin password -- those I leave without defaults on purpose, and I mark the password @secure() on top of that. I want the pipeline to be forced to pull that value from somewhere secure every time, not accidentally succeed with a stale or hardcoded credential nobody noticed was still sitting there as a fallback.
commonMistakes: Giving sqlAdminPassword a default value (even a blank placeholder), undermining the point of requiring it explicitly each deployment
Forgetting the @secure() decorator on the password parameter, exposing it in deployment history
Using an overly broad firewall IP range instead of the 0.0.0.0-0.0.0.0 'Allow Azure services' convention
Hardcoding the database SKU instead of exposing it as a parameter
Assuming a parameter with a default still forces the pipeline to supply a value
keyPoints: A defaulted parameter is optional; the deployment silently falls back to the default if omitted
A non-defaulted parameter is required; validation fails immediately if it's missing
In non-interactive CI/CD, there's no prompt to recover from a missing required value -- it simply fails fast
Secrets like the admin password should be required (no default) and marked @secure()
Standard, non-sensitive values like location or SKU are reasonable candidates for defaults

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Bicep resources (SQL server, database, firewall rule)
Correct parameterization of server name, admin login/password, SKU, and IP range
Correct @secure() usage on the password parameter
Accurately explains optional-vs-required parameter behavior at deployment time
Explains why secrets should never have defaults in a CI/CD context

questions.title: A JDBC Source Connector Config, and What Connect's Offsets Topic Actually Tracks
questions.prompt: Write the JSON configuration for a Kafka Connect source connector that pulls new rows from a JDBC database table into a Kafka topic, incrementing off a numeric ID column, including the converter settings for the data written to the topic. Then explain precisely what Kafka Connect's internal offsets topic is tracking for this connector, and how that's different from what a downstream consumer group's committed offsets track for the same destination topic.
questions.modelAnswer:
The connector config declares connector.class as the JDBC source connector, mode set to incrementing with incrementing.column.name naming the strictly-increasing numeric column the connector polls against, table.whitelist (or table.include.list on newer versions) naming the source table, topic.prefix controlling the destination topic name, and key.converter/value.converter defining how rows get serialized onto that topic.

Kafka Connect's internal offsets topic (named via offset.storage.topic for a distributed worker, often connect-offsets) is not tracking Kafka partition offsets on the destination topic at all -- for a source connector, 'offset' means the connector's own position within the source system it's reading from. For this incrementing-mode JDBC connector specifically, what gets persisted there is the last-seen value of the incrementing column (the highest ID the connector has successfully read and produced), keyed by the connector's own source partition (effectively, per table/query it's tracking). That's what lets the connector resume correctly after a restart or a task reassignment: it reads that last value back out of the offsets topic and resumes its query with something equivalent to WHERE id > last_seen_id, with zero relationship to any Kafka topic-partition offset number.

A downstream consumer group's committed offsets are tracking something entirely different: they live in Kafka's own __consumer_offsets topic, and for each topic-partition a given consumer group is reading, they record the last Kafka log offset (a monotonically increasing position within that specific partition's log) that group has successfully processed. That's purely about progress through the Kafka topic Connect produced into -- it has no awareness of, or relationship to, where Connect itself left off pulling from the source database. The two mechanisms happen to both be called 'offsets' and both get persisted to internal Kafka topics, but one answers 'where did I leave off reading the source system' and the other answers 'where did I leave off reading this Kafka partition' -- entirely separate systems being tracked, entirely separate storage.
questions.professionalAnswer:
For the connector config itself, I'd set connector.class to the JDBC source connector, mode to incrementing with incrementing.column.name pointing at whatever numeric ID column is strictly increasing, name the source table, set a topic.prefix so I know exactly which topic the rows land in, and configure the converters for however I want the data serialized going out.

The part people mix up is what Connect's own offsets topic is actually storing. It sounds like it should be the same kind of 'offset' you'd see on a Kafka topic-partition, but for a source connector it's completely different -- it's the connector's bookmark in the source system, not in Kafka. For this JDBC incrementing connector, that bookmark is literally just 'the highest ID value I've successfully pulled so far,' and that's what gets persisted so that when the connector restarts, it knows to resume querying from there rather than starting over or skipping ahead.

A consumer group's committed offsets are a totally separate concept that just happens to share the word. Those live in __consumer_offsets, and they're tracking, per topic-partition, the last Kafka log position some consumer group has actually processed -- that's purely about reading the Kafka topic Connect wrote into, with zero awareness of where Connect itself left off in the source database. So you've got two different 'offset' bookkeeping systems doing two unrelated jobs: one tracks progress through the upstream source, the other tracks progress through the downstream Kafka log.
questions.example:
{
  "name": "jdbc-source-orders",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.confluent.connect.jdbc.JdbcSourceConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "connection.url": "jdbc:sqlserver://sqlserver.internal:1433;databaseName=Sales",
    "connection.user": "kafka_connect_svc",
    "connection.password": "${file:/secrets/jdbc-creds.properties:password}",
    "mode": "incrementing",
    "incrementing.column.name": "OrderID",
    "table.whitelist": "Orders",
    "topic.prefix": "sqlserver-",
    "poll.interval.ms": "5000",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "value.converter": "io.confluent.connect.avro.AvroConverter",
    "value.converter.schema.registry.url": "http://schema-registry:8081"
  }
}
commonMistakes: Assuming Connect's offsets topic stores destination Kafka topic-partition offsets rather than source-system position
Using mode incrementing without realizing it only captures new rows, missing updates or deletes on existing rows
Putting the database password in plain text in the connector JSON instead of referencing a config provider or secret store
Omitting poll.interval.ms and accepting a default polling cadence that doesn't match the actual data arrival rate
Confusing Connect's internal offset.storage.topic with the destination data topic the connector writes rows into
keyPoints: connector.class, mode, and incrementing.column.name define how and what rows are pulled from the source
topic.prefix controls the destination Kafka topic name
key.converter/value.converter define the serialization format of data written to that topic
Connect's internal offsets topic stores source-system position (e.g. last incrementing ID seen), not Kafka topic-partition offsets
A consumer group's committed offsets, stored in __consumer_offsets, track progress through the Kafka topic itself
These are two unrelated bookkeeping systems that happen to share the word 'offset'

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct connector JSON config (class, mode, incrementing column, topic prefix)
Correct converter configuration
Correctly explains what Connect's offsets topic stores for a source connector
Correctly contrasts this with a consumer group's committed offsets
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline Table with a Drop-Row Expectation, and Drop vs. Fail Semantics
questions.prompt: Define a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline table (the framework most engineers still know by its earlier name, Delta Live Tables / @dlt.table) that reads from a raw orders dataset and enforces a data-quality rule rejecting any row where order_total is negative or null, dropping only the bad rows rather than failing the whole table. Then explain precisely how that drop-row expectation behaves differently from configuring the identical rule to fail the pipeline run instead, including what happens to the rows involved in each case and what gets recorded in the pipeline's metrics.
questions.modelAnswer:
An expectation configured to drop (expect_or_drop in Python, ON VIOLATION DROP ROW in SQL) attaches a named constraint to the dataset's definition. When a row violates the predicate, that single row is silently removed before anything gets written to the target table -- it never appears in clean_orders -- but every other row in that batch or micro-batch continues through completely normally, and the table update as a whole still completes and commits successfully. The pipeline's run metrics (visible in the pipeline UI's data-quality panel, and in the underlying event log) record exactly how many rows that specific named constraint dropped, giving ongoing visibility into how much bad data is being absorbed without it ever blocking anything downstream.

Configuring the identical predicate to fail instead (expect_or_fail in Python, ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE in SQL) behaves completely differently, not just more strictly. The moment a single row violates the rule, the flow updating that table halts with an exception, and because Lakeflow table writes are transactional, the entire update for that run is rolled back atomically -- meaning none of the rows from that run commit to the target table, not merely the offending one. There's no meaningful drop-count metric recorded for a fail, because the update never reaches a committed state for metrics to be captured against; what you get instead is a failed pipeline run that has to be investigated and rerun once the underlying data or the rule itself is fixed.

There's a third option worth contrasting against both: a plain expectation with no violation action (expect in Python, a bare EXPECT in SQL) neither drops nor fails anything -- it keeps every row, bad or good, and only records pass/fail counts for visibility. Choosing between drop, fail, and warn-only is really a judgment call about how much the business can tolerate a known rate of bad data flowing through versus needing a hard stop the moment it appears.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I think about these three expectation modes as three completely different risk postures, not three strengths of the same thing. expect_or_drop is the one to reach for when I expect a small, known rate of genuinely bad rows and I'd rather quietly filter them out and keep the pipeline moving -- the bad row just never makes it into the output table, everything else in that batch sails through fine, and the table update still commits normally. The pipeline UI shows me exactly how many rows that specific rule caught, so I'm never flying blind about how much is getting filtered.

expect_or_fail is a completely different animal, and I'm careful not to use it as if it's just a stricter version of drop. The instant one row breaks that rule, the whole update for that run gets rolled back -- not just the bad row, everything from that run, because the write is transactional. So if someone's expecting 'the good 999 rows still get through and only the 1 bad one gets blocked,' that's not what fail does at all -- it's all or nothing, and there's no drop-count metric to look at afterward because the update never actually committed for metrics to be recorded against. And then there's the plain expect with no action attached, which I use purely for observability -- it doesn't touch the data at all, good or bad, it just tracks how many rows would have passed or failed if I'd chosen one of the other two.
commonMistakes: Using expect_or_fail when the real intent was to quietly drop a small, expected rate of bad rows, halting the pipeline over normal data noise
Using a plain expect (warn-only) when the intent was actually to keep bad rows out of the target table -- it records metrics but removes nothing
Assuming a failed expectation still commits the good rows from that run; the entire update rolls back, not just the bad row
Forgetting the expectation decorator/constraint must be attached directly to the same table definition it's meant to guard
Never checking the pipeline's data-quality metrics to see how many rows a drop constraint is actually removing over time
keyPoints: expect_or_drop removes only the violating rows; the rest of the batch and the table update succeed normally
expect_or_fail halts and atomically rolls back the entire update on the first violation -- zero rows commit from that run, not just the bad one
Drop-row counts are recorded in pipeline metrics; a fail produces no such metric because the update never commits
A plain expect (no violation action) only records pass/fail metrics and never blocks or removes any row
The module is now pyspark.pipelines (imported as dp), though the earlier dlt module and @dlt.table syntax still work unchanged

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct table definition with an expect_or_drop (or ON VIOLATION DROP ROW) constraint enforcing the rule
Correctly explains that drop removes only violating rows while the rest of the update succeeds
Correctly explains fail's atomic rollback of the entire update, not just the offending row
Correctly distinguishes metrics recorded for drop vs. none for a failed update
Mentions plain expect (warn-only) as a third option for contrast
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Walking a Bill-of-Materials Hierarchy with a Recursive CTE
questions.prompt: AdventureWorks2012's Production.BillOfMaterials table models a bicycle's bill of materials: a top-level assembly (ProductAssemblyID) is built from component products (ComponentID), and some of those components are themselves sub-assemblies built from further components, to an unknown depth. Write a query that returns the full multi-level component tree for a given assembly, including each component's depth level, using only currently-active BOM rows. Then explain the two required parts of a recursive CTE, why one particular set operator is mandatory, and what safety valve you'd put in place before running this against unfamiliar data.
questions.modelAnswer:
A recursive CTE has exactly two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member that seeds the recursion (here, the direct components of the requested assembly), and a recursive member that references the CTE by its own name and joins the next level down onto the previous pass's results. SQL Server keeps re-executing the recursive member, feeding each pass's output back in as input to the next, until a pass produces zero new rows -- that's the only termination condition, which is exactly why cyclic data (a component that is, transitively, its own ancestor) can spin forever without a guard.

UNION ALL is mandatory, not a style choice: SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax does not permit plain UNION for the member union, because UNION's deduplication would have to compare against the full accumulated result set on every pass, which conflicts with how the recursive expansion is implemented. You also cannot put TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE itself inside the recursive member -- the recursive member is restricted to a simple SELECT...FROM CTE JOIN base-table shape.

The safety valve is OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) on the outer statement. The default limit is 100 levels; set it explicitly (or to 0, meaning unlimited, only when you're certain the data is acyclic) so a bad BOM row with a circular reference fails fast with error 530 instead of running away. Finally, filter EndDate IS NULL in both the anchor and the recursive member's join predicate -- Production.BillOfMaterials keeps historical, retired component relationships, and without that filter the hierarchy walk includes assemblies that no longer apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a recursive CTE here because this is a classic parent-child walk of unknown depth -- you can't write a fixed number of self-joins when you don't know how many sub-assembly levels exist. I'd structure it as an anchor that grabs the direct components of the assembly I'm given, filtered to EndDate IS NULL so I'm not pulling in retired BOM relationships, starting at level zero. Then the recursive part joins BillOfMaterials back onto the CTE itself, matching the previous level's ComponentID to the new row's ProductAssemblyID, bumping the level each time. I always remind people UNION ALL isn't optional there -- SQL Server's recursive CTE syntax simply won't accept a plain UNION on that join. And before I'd run this against a BOM table I didn't already trust, I'd tack on OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100) or some sane number, because if there's ever a circular reference in that data -- a component that loops back to one of its own ancestors -- I want a clean error, not a query that just hangs.
questions.example:
WITH BOMHierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor: direct components of the requested assembly
    SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, 0 AS Level,
           CAST(ComponentID AS VARCHAR(400)) AS Path
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials
    WHERE ProductAssemblyID = 800 AND EndDate IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive member: references BOMHierarchy by its own name
    SELECT bom.ProductAssemblyID, bom.ComponentID, bh.Level + 1,
           bh.Path + '/' + CAST(bom.ComponentID AS VARCHAR(20))
    FROM Production.BillOfMaterials AS bom
    INNER JOIN BOMHierarchy AS bh
        ON bom.ProductAssemblyID = bh.ComponentID
    WHERE bom.EndDate IS NULL
)
SELECT ProductAssemblyID, ComponentID, Level, Path
FROM BOMHierarchy
ORDER BY Level
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);
commonMistakes: Using UNION instead of UNION ALL, which T-SQL rejects for recursive CTEs
Forgetting to filter EndDate IS NULL, pulling in retired BOM relationships
Not setting MAXRECURSION, so a circular reference in the data hangs instead of erroring cleanly
Assuming the CTE itself is indexed or materialized, when it's really re-expanded pass by pass
Putting DISTINCT, TOP, or an outer join against the CTE inside the recursive member, which T-SQL disallows
keyPoints: Anchor member seeds the recursion; recursive member references the CTE by its own name
UNION ALL is required between anchor and recursive member -- plain UNION is disallowed
Recursion stops automatically when a pass produces zero new rows
OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) is the safety valve against circular/cyclic data
Filter EndDate IS NULL to exclude retired BOM relationships
The recursive member cannot contain TOP, DISTINCT, GROUP BY/HAVING, or an outer join against the CTE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct anchor/recursive member structure in the query
Explains why UNION ALL is mandatory, not a preference
Addresses recursion depth/cycle safety via MAXRECURSION
Filters to active BOM rows (EndDate IS NULL)
Correctly describes recursive CTE syntax restrictions
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Removing Duplicate Staging Rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
questions.prompt: A failed, partially-retried ETL load left Staging.SalesOrderDetail with duplicate rows sharing the same (SalesOrderID, ProductID), each with a different SalesOrderDetailID. Write a set-based query that deletes every duplicate except the one with the lowest SalesOrderDetailID for each key combination. Then explain why this approach is preferred over a cursor-based row-by-row deletion, and what would change in your query if you needed to keep the duplicate with the highest, rather than lowest, SalesOrderDetailID.
questions.modelAnswer:
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) is the right tool because it assigns a unique, strictly sequential number to every row within each partition without collapsing any rows the way GROUP BY would -- each duplicate row survives in the result set, just tagged with its position within its own (SalesOrderID, ProductID) group, ordered however I specify. Wrapping that in a CTE lets me then DELETE directly against the CTE wherever the assigned row number is greater than 1 -- SQL Server treats the CTE as a view onto the same underlying rows, so deleting from it deletes the real staging rows.

This beats a cursor for the same reason any row-by-row approach loses to a set-based one: a cursor would FETCH one row at a time, decide whether to delete it, and round-trip through the query engine's overhead for every single row -- on a staging table with any real volume, that's dramatically slower than a single set-based operation the engine can plan and execute as one pass (or a small number of passes) over the data, using whatever indexes exist on the partition/order columns.

To keep the highest SalesOrderDetailID instead of the lowest, the only change needed is the ORDER BY inside OVER(): ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC instead of ascending (or no direction, since ascending is the default) -- row number 1 then lands on the highest ID in each partition, and everything else (the PARTITION BY, the DELETE WHERE rn > 1) stays identical. It's worth noting RANK() or DENSE_RANK() would be the wrong choice here specifically because they assign the same rank to true ties -- I want exactly one designated "keeper" row per key no matter what, which is precisely what ROW_NUMBER()'s strict, no-ties-allowed numbering guarantees.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move is to reach for ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the duplicate key -- SalesOrderID and ProductID together -- ordered by SalesOrderDetailID ascending, so within each duplicate group the row I want to keep gets numbered 1 and everything else gets 2, 3, and so on. I put that inside a CTE, and then I can delete straight from the CTE wherever that row number is greater than one -- SQL Server lets you do that because the CTE is really just a lens onto the same underlying staging rows.

I'd explain to someone why I didn't write this as a cursor: a cursor processes one row at a time, and every one of those iterations carries its own overhead -- that's exactly the row-by-row anti-pattern this course warns about. SQL Server's engine is built to work on whole sets of rows at once, so a single set-based DELETE against the CTE lets the optimizer handle this as one efficient operation instead of forcing it into thousands of tiny ones.

And if someone asked me to flip it around and keep the highest ID instead of the lowest, that's a one-word change -- just add DESC to the ORDER BY inside the OVER() clause. I'd also mention I specifically didn't reach for RANK or DENSE_RANK here, because those can tie two rows at the same rank, and I need exactly one row designated as the keeper every time -- ROW_NUMBER is the only one of the three that guarantees that.
questions.example:
WITH Duplicates AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY SalesOrderID, ProductID
               ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM Staging.SalesOrderDetail
)
DELETE FROM Duplicates
WHERE rn > 1;

-- To keep the HIGHEST SalesOrderDetailID instead, only the ORDER BY direction changes:
-- ORDER BY SalesOrderDetailID DESC
commonMistakes: Using a cursor or WHILE loop to delete duplicates row by row
Using RANK() or DENSE_RANK() instead of ROW_NUMBER(), which can tie and leave more than one 'keeper' row
Forgetting that DELETE works against the CTE because it's a direct view onto the base rows, not a copy
Omitting an explicit ORDER BY inside OVER(), leaving which row survives undefined
Running the DELETE without first running the SELECT version to verify which rows would be removed
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) numbers every row without collapsing the result set
DELETE can run directly against a CTE wrapping the window function
Set-based deletion beats row-by-row cursor processing for performance at volume
ROW_NUMBER guarantees a single keeper per partition; RANK/DENSE_RANK do not
Flipping ASC/DESC in the ORDER BY changes which duplicate is kept

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ROW_NUMBER/PARTITION BY/DELETE query
Explains why set-based beats cursor-based deletion
Correctly identifies the ORDER BY change needed to keep the highest ID
Explains why ROW_NUMBER is preferred over RANK/DENSE_RANK here
Clear, accurate overall explanation

questions.title: Designing a Covering, Filtered Index for a High-Frequency Reporting Query
questions.prompt: A reporting endpoint runs this query hundreds of times per minute: SELECT ProductID, Name, ListPrice FROM Production.Product WHERE Color = 'Red' AND SellEndDate IS NULL ORDER BY ListPrice. Design the single nonclustered index you'd create to best serve it -- specifying key column order, included columns, and any filter -- and explain exactly how you'd confirm in the execution plan that it's actually being used as a fully covering seek rather than falling back to a scan or a key lookup.
questions.modelAnswer:
The query filters on Color (equality) and SellEndDate IS NULL, then orders by ListPrice, and selects ProductID, Name, ListPrice. I'd build the index key on Color first, since it's the equality predicate the optimizer can seek on directly, then ListPrice second, since that both satisfies part of the ORDER BY and keeps rows pre-sorted within each color -- letting the engine potentially avoid a separate sort operator entirely. ProductID and Name don't belong in the key at all; they're only ever selected, never filtered or sorted on, so they belong as INCLUDE columns, which attaches their data to the index's leaf level without making them part of the search key (keeping the key itself narrow). Finally, since this query only ever cares about currently-active products, I'd add a filter: WHERE SellEndDate IS NULL, so the index only covers the subset of rows this specific query pattern actually needs -- smaller, faster to scan, and still perfectly usable by any other query matching that same filter condition.

To confirm it's working as intended, I'd turn on the actual execution plan (Ctrl+M) and run the exact production query. I'm looking for a single Index Seek operator with no accompanying Key Lookup and no separate Sort operator afterward -- that combination means the index is fully covering (every selected column came straight from the index, no trip back to the clustered index) and pre-sorted for the ORDER BY. If I instead see an Index Seek followed by a Key Lookup, that tells me I missed an included column the query actually needs. If I see a Sort operator after the seek, either my key column order doesn't match the ORDER BY the way I assumed, or the optimizer decided sorting was cheaper than using the index's physical order for some other reason. And if I see a Scan instead of a Seek at all, I'd first check that the filter predicate on the index exactly matches the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server will only use a filtered index when it can prove the query's predicate is a subset of the index's filter, and a subtle mismatch (like comparing against a variable instead of a literal in some SQL Server versions) can silently prevent that match and fall back to scanning the base table.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Walking through the query, I see one equality filter (Color), one IS NULL filter that's really describing 'currently active products' (SellEndDate), an ORDER BY on ListPrice, and three columns actually being selected. So my index key is Color first, because that's the equality predicate, then ListPrice second, because that handles the sort and keeps things grouped nicely within each color. ProductID and Name never show up in a WHERE or ORDER BY here, so I don't want them cluttering the key -- they go in as INCLUDE columns instead, just along for the ride so the index can hand back the full row without touching the base table. And since this query only ever wants active products, I'd make the whole index filtered on SellEndDate IS NULL -- there's no reason to carry the weight of retired products in an index built specifically for this access pattern.

To prove it's actually helping, I turn on the actual plan and run the real query, and I want to see exactly one operator: an Index Seek, nothing else hanging off it. If there's a Key Lookup tagging along, that tells me I forgot to include a column the query needed. If there's a Sort sitting after the seek, my key order isn't lining up with the ORDER BY the way I thought it would. And if I'm staring at a Scan instead of a Seek, my first suspicion is that the filter on the index doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause -- SQL Server is strict about that match for a filtered index, and small mismatches are a classic reason the optimizer quietly falls back to ignoring it.
commonMistakes: Putting ProductID/Name in the index key instead of as INCLUDE columns, widening the key unnecessarily
Forgetting the ORDER BY column when choosing key column order, leaving a Sort in the plan
Leaving off the filter, indexing retired products the query never actually needs
Assuming an Index Seek alone proves full coverage without checking for an accompanying Key Lookup
Writing a filter predicate that doesn't exactly match the query's WHERE clause, causing SQL Server to ignore the filtered index
keyPoints: Equality predicate columns go first in the index key, ahead of sort/range columns
ORDER BY columns in the key can eliminate a separate Sort operator
Select-only columns belong in INCLUDE, not the key, to keep the key narrow
A filtered index should match the query's WHERE clause as closely as possible
Verify with the actual execution plan: single seek, no Key Lookup, no Sort = fully covering

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct key column choice and order (Color, ListPrice)
Correctly places ProductID/Name as INCLUDE columns
Correctly applies the SellEndDate IS NULL filter
Describes verifying via actual execution plan (seek, no key lookup, no sort)
Explains what a Key Lookup or Sort in the plan would each indicate is wrong

questions.title: Fix the Non-SARGable Order Lookup
questions.prompt: The query below is used in a nightly dashboard refresh and is now the slowest query in the job, taking almost 4 minutes against the Orders table (60M rows, nonclustered index on OrderDate). Rewrite it so it can use an index seek instead of a scan, without changing what it returns.
questions.code:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) = '2026-03-15'
   OR DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) = '2026-03-16';
questions.modelAnswer: This query has two separate non-SARGable predicates combined with OR, each of which independently forces a full scan: CONVERT(varchar(10), OrderDate, 120) wraps the column in a string conversion before comparing it, and DATEADD(day, 1, OrderDate) performs arithmetic on the column before comparing it — both require per-row evaluation across all 60 million rows, and the OR compounds the cost further because the optimizer can't cleanly combine two non-seekable branches into a single seek plan. Both predicates are actually expressing the exact same intent (rows where OrderDate falls on March 15, 2026), so the correct fix is to collapse them into a single SARGable range predicate that leaves OrderDate bare on one side of the comparison, using a half-open interval to correctly capture the entire day regardless of time-of-day values stored in the column.
questions.professionalAnswer: Looking at this, both of these predicates are just two different, overcomplicated ways of saying 'OrderDate is March 15th, 2026' — one converts the column to a string and compares it to a string literal, the other adds a day and compares to the 16th, and both of those operations have to run against the column before SQL Server can even check the condition, which means it can't seek, it has to scan every row and compute the expression first. I'd collapse this down to a plain date range using the raw column, written as a half-open interval so it still works correctly even if OrderDate has a time component — that keeps the column bare on the left side of the comparison so the optimizer can seek straight into the nonclustered index on OrderDate instead of touching all 60 million rows.
questions.example:
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, TotalAmount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-03-15'
  AND OrderDate < '2026-03-16';

Using OrderDate = '2026-03-15' directly, which silently misses rows with a non-midnight time component
Not recognizing that both predicates express the same logical condition and can be merged into one range
Adding an index hint instead of fixing the predicate, which doesn't solve the underlying non-SARGable issue
Forgetting the half-open interval pattern and using BETWEEN with an inclusive end date/time that can miss late-day rows
keyPoints: Both original predicates wrap the column in a function/arithmetic, forcing per-row evaluation and a scan
Recognize that both branches express the same underlying date condition
Rewrite as a single SARGable half-open range on the bare column
Half-open range correctly handles any time-of-day component on OrderDate
Resulting plan should allow an index seek on the nonclustered OrderDate index

Produces a correct, equivalent SARGable rewrite

Explains expected improvement (seek vs scan)
