questions.title: Design a Tumbling Window Pipeline With Retry and Alerting
questions.prompt: You need an Azure Data Factory pipeline that ingests hourly batch files from a partner into Azure Data Lake, processes each hour's file exactly once even if the pipeline is paused and resumed, and alerts the team on repeated failure without manual babysitting. Describe the trigger type, retry configuration, and failure-handling pattern you'd configure, and explain why a tumbling window trigger is the right choice over a simple schedule trigger here.
questions.modelAnswer: A tumbling window trigger is the correct choice because it is explicitly designed around fixed, non-overlapping time windows that each get their own tracked execution state and window start/end time (@trigger().outputs.windowStartTime / windowEndTime), which lets the pipeline know precisely which hour's file it should be processing for that run, and critically, it supports dependency and retry semantics plus automatic backfill: if the pipeline is paused for several hours and then resumed, the tumbling window trigger will automatically queue and execute the missed windows in order, each exactly once, rather than simply skipping ahead to 'now' the way a plain schedule trigger would. A schedule trigger fires at wall-clock times with no concept of windows or backfill — if it's paused, those fire times are simply lost, and there's no built-in mechanism tying a given run to 'which hour's file' beyond what you manually derive from the trigger time, making exactly-once-per-hour semantics much harder to guarantee. For retry, I'd configure the trigger's own retryPolicy (count and interval) for transient failures at the trigger level, and additionally configure the Copy Activity's own retry count/interval for transient source/sink connectivity issues, since activity-level retries handle smaller transient hiccups without re-running the entire pipeline. For failure handling and alerting, I'd attach a failure-path activity (via the 'on failure' dependency condition in the pipeline canvas) that runs after the main activities only if they fail, which calls a Logic App or Azure Function to post to Teams/email, or more directly, configure an Azure Monitor alert rule on the Data Factory's own PipelineFailedRuns metric so the team gets paged without needing custom alerting logic embedded in every pipeline.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for a tumbling window trigger here specifically because of the backfill and exactly-once guarantees it gives you, which a plain schedule trigger just doesn't have. A schedule trigger is basically a clock — it fires at set wall-clock times, and if the pipeline's paused when a fire time comes around, that execution is just gone, there's no catch-up. A tumbling window trigger instead tracks discrete time windows, each with its own state, so if I pause it for six hours and then resume, it knows exactly which windows it missed and it'll queue them up and run them in order, each one exactly once — which is exactly the 'process each hour's file exactly once even after a pause' requirement here. Inside the pipeline, I'd use the trigger's own windowStartTime and windowEndTime parameters to construct the exact filename or path for that hour's partner file, so there's no ambiguity about which window a given run corresponds to. For retries, I'd set them at two levels — a retry policy on the trigger itself for the pipeline as a whole, and separately a retry count on the Copy Activity itself, since a lot of these partner-file failures are transient network blips that resolve themselves on a quick retry without needing to escalate. And for the 'alert without babysitting' part, I wouldn't build custom alerting logic inside the pipeline — I'd set an Azure Monitor alert rule directly against Data Factory's pipeline failure metrics, so once retries are exhausted and a run is truly failed, it pages the team through whatever channel they already use, rather than relying on someone checking the monitoring tab.
commonMistakes: Choosing a schedule trigger and manually trying to reconstruct 'which hour' logic from current wall-clock time
Assuming a paused schedule trigger will automatically backfill missed runs the way a tumbling window trigger does
Only configuring retries at the activity level and ignoring trigger-level retry policy, or vice versa
Building custom email/Teams alerting inside every pipeline instead of using Azure Monitor alert rules on Data Factory metrics
Not using windowStartTime/windowEndTime to deterministically identify which file/partition a given run should process
keyPoints: Tumbling window trigger tracks discrete, stateful time windows with automatic backfill on resume
windowStartTime/windowEndTime deterministically identify which hour's data a run should process
Retry should be configured at both the trigger level and the activity level for different failure classes
Azure Monitor alert rules on Data Factory metrics provide alerting without custom in-pipeline logic
Schedule triggers lack windowing/backfill semantics, making exactly-once-per-period harder to guarantee

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly justifies tumbling window trigger over schedule trigger with backfill/windowing reasoning
Correctly describes retry configuration at trigger and activity levels
Correctly describes a sound failure-alerting pattern
Uses windowStartTime/windowEndTime correctly to identify the processing window
Clarity and completeness

questions.title: A Dashboard-Facing Delta Table Has Quietly Degraded From Small Files
questions.prompt: A Delta table feeding several BI dashboards has been append-only, ingested every 15 minutes by a streaming job for the last 8 months. Row count has only grown about 20% in that time, the query the dashboards run hasn't changed, but the same query that used to return in 3 seconds now takes 3-4 minutes. Nobody on the team has ever run OPTIMIZE or VACUUM on this table. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it, and how you'd prove the fix worked.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd confirm the symptom is really a small-file problem before touching anything, rather than assuming. Running DESCRIBE DETAIL on the table gives numFiles and sizeInBytes directly, and dividing those two gives average file size. If that number comes back in the tens or low hundreds of KB on a table this size and age, that's a hard confirmation, not a guess -- the recommended Delta file size for good query performance is generally in the 128MB-1GB range depending on table size.

The root cause is mechanical once you see the file count: a streaming job appending every 15 minutes for 8 months is roughly 23,000 micro-batches, and each micro-batch writes at least one new Parquet file, often more depending on partitioning and task parallelism. With OPTIMIZE never run, file count scales with how often the job fired, not with how much data arrived -- those are two completely different axes. That's exactly why a 20% row-count increase and a 60-80x runtime increase don't correlate: the thing that actually got worse is file count, not data volume.

Why that hurts dashboard queries specifically: the query engine has to open, read the footer of, and schedule a task for every single file, and at hundreds of thousands to over a million files that per-file overhead -- especially against cloud object storage with per-request latency -- dwarfs the actual time spent scanning 40GB of real data. The Delta transaction log itself also gets more expensive to plan against with that many file entries recorded across its history.

The fix is OPTIMIZE to compact the small files into right-sized ones, but a one-time compaction alone just resets the clock on the same problem recurring in another few months. I'd also enable delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite and delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact as table properties (or move to liquid clustering if the runtime supports it) so new small files get compacted automatically going forward instead of silently accumulating again. I'd run VACUUM afterward too, but I'd be precise about what it does: VACUUM only removes files that are no longer referenced after the retention window (default 7 days) to reclaim storage and reduce the file-listing surface -- it has no effect on query speed on its own, so running VACUUM without OPTIMIZE would not have fixed this at all.

To verify, I'd re-run DESCRIBE DETAIL and show the before/after on numFiles and average file size, then re-run the actual dashboard query and compare wall-clock time and Spark UI task counts/bytes read before and after -- that's the real proof, not just a feeling that it's faster.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The row-count math is the tell for me before I even open a notebook -- rows grew 20%, runtime grew 60-80x, so whatever's slow isn't proportional to data volume, which means it's probably proportional to something else: file count. I'd go straight to DESCRIBE DETAIL and look at numFiles versus sizeInBytes, because dividing those two gives me average file size, and if that number is sitting in the tens or hundreds of KB on a table this old, that's my answer right there.

What actually happened is pretty mechanical: this table's been fed by a streaming job every 15 minutes for eight months, and every one of those roughly 23,000 micro-batches wrote at least one new file. Nobody ever ran OPTIMIZE, so the file count scaled with how often the job ran, not with how much data came in -- those are two completely different axes, which is exactly why the row-count growth and the slowdown don't match.

Why that kills a dashboard specifically: every query has to open, read the footer of, and schedule a task for each of those files, and at over a million files that per-file overhead swamps the actual work of scanning 40GB of data. The transaction log itself has also gotten heavier to plan against with that many file entries.

The fix is OPTIMIZE, but I wouldn't stop there -- a one-time compaction just resets the clock on the same problem recurring. I'd turn on autoOptimize.optimizeWrite and autoCompact (or move to liquid clustering if the runtime supports it) so this doesn't quietly come back in another eight months. And I'd be careful not to conflate this with VACUUM -- VACUUM is a storage cleanup step that removes files no longer referenced after the retention window, it has zero effect on query speed, so running it alone wouldn't have fixed anything here.

To prove it worked, I'd show the before/after on numFiles and average file size directly, and then the actual dashboard query time, not just 'it feels faster.'
commonMistakes: Assuming row-count growth explains the slowdown and never checking file count or average file size at all
Running VACUUM expecting it to speed up queries, when it only reclaims storage after the retention window
Running OPTIMIZE once but never enabling auto-optimize/auto-compact, so the problem quietly returns in a few more months
Choosing a Z-ORDER column that doesn't match the dashboard's actual filter columns, which doesn't address the core small-file issue
Jumping straight to resizing the cluster instead of looking at file layout first
keyPoints: DESCRIBE DETAIL's numFiles and average file size is the correct diagnostic signal, not row count
Root cause: many small files from frequent streaming appends that were never compacted
OPTIMIZE compacts files and improves query speed; VACUUM only reclaims storage after retention and doesn't touch query speed
Prevent recurrence with autoOptimize.optimizeWrite/autoCompact or liquid clustering
Verify with before/after numFiles, average file size, and actual query wall-clock time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Uses DESCRIBE DETAIL / file count and size to confirm the small-file problem
Correctly explains the root cause (frequent small appends never compacted)
Prescribes OPTIMIZE as the fix
Distinguishes OPTIMIZE's query benefit from VACUUM's storage-only benefit
Proposes prevention (auto-optimize) and concrete before/after verification

questions.title: Autoloader Started Silently Skipping Files After a Storage Lifecycle Policy Change
questions.prompt: An Autoloader stream ingests hourly JSON files into a Delta table, running on a job cluster that starts and terminates each hour. A few weeks ago the storage team added an account-wide lifecycle rule that deletes any blob older than 30 days, including blobs under the stream's checkpoint location, to save on storage cost. A monthly reconciliation just found that a handful of source files over the last six weeks were never ingested into the table, with no errors, warnings, or failed runs anywhere in the job history. Walk through why Autoloader's checkpoint and file-tracking design makes it vulnerable to exactly this, and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
First I'd rule out the obvious, loud failure mode: malformed or schema-mismatched records. Autoloader's rescue mechanism and bad-records handling leave visible evidence -- a rescued-data column, entries at a configured badRecordsPath, or schema-evolution failures that stop the stream. Since there's zero evidence of any of that and the job history shows clean, successful runs the whole time, that rules out a data-quality skip and points at something structural in how the stream tracks its own progress.

The actual mechanism: a checkpoint location holds more than the standard Structured Streaming offset and commit logs. Autoloader also maintains its own file-tracking state there -- a RocksDB-backed record of which source files have already been seen and enqueued, used by directory-listing mode to avoid reprocessing or losing track of progress. All of that, plus the offset/commit delta log, is written as a long series of small log segments that Spark intends to periodically compact (by default roughly every 10 batches) into a durable snapshot, but which are otherwise expected to persist indefinitely -- they are not disposable application logs.

A blanket 30-day age-based lifecycle rule has no concept of any of that; it deletes blob segments purely by age, regardless of whether Structured Streaming has rolled them into a compacted snapshot yet. Because this job runs on an auto-terminating hourly job cluster, the stream has to fully reconstruct its state from whatever remains in the checkpoint path on every single run. If pieces of that state -- especially the older RocksDB segments or uncompacted offset/commit deltas -- get deleted before a compaction consumed them, recovery can end up with an incomplete picture of what's genuinely still pending versus already processed. In practice that surfaces not as a crash but as the listing high-water mark silently advancing past files that were sitting in the source directory but had not actually been ingested, because the piece of state that would have still flagged them as pending was the piece that got deleted.

To confirm this cheaply: correlate the specific missing files' arrival timestamps against the lifecycle policy's 30-day cutoff and the job's hourly restart cadence, and check the storage account's lifecycle/management policy and its delete activity logs scoped to the checkpoint container or prefix.

The fix has two parts and both matter. First, exclude the checkpoint location (and the Autoloader schema location, if separate) from any lifecycle/retention policy entirely -- those paths need to persist indefinitely and should only ever be managed by Spark or Databricks' own mechanisms. Second, backfill the files that already fell through the gap: simply restarting the stream will not retroactively pick them up, since whatever high-water mark the stream now holds has already moved past them. A one-time scoped batch read using Autoloader with modifiedAfter/modifiedBefore file filters covering the gap window, written into the same Delta table, recovers the missing data. I'd verify by reconciling the full source file inventory against the table afterward, and add an ongoing count-based alert so a future silent gap surfaces immediately rather than at the next manual reconciliation.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first instinct whenever Autoloader drops files is to check for the loud, well-known failure mode -- malformed records getting rescued or routed to a bad-records path -- but the fact that this is completely silent, with zero evidence anywhere, tells me it's not that. Malformed data leaves a trail; this didn't.

So I'd go to what actually lives in a checkpoint directory, because people tend to think of it as just 'where Spark remembers its offset,' and that's only half of it. Autoloader keeps its own file-tracking state there too -- a RocksDB-backed record of which source files it's already seen and enqueued -- and that state, along with the standard offset and commit logs, is written as a long series of small log segments that are meant to be periodically compacted, not aged out by a generic cleanup rule.

That's exactly what collides with a 30-day lifecycle policy applied blindly across the whole storage account. It doesn't know those files are special; it just deletes anything old. If this job runs on a cluster that spins up and down every hour, it has to fully reload its state from whatever's left in that checkpoint path on every single run -- so if pieces of that state got swept away before Spark had compacted them into a durable snapshot, recovery can end up with an incomplete picture of what's actually been processed, and in practice that surfaces as files quietly falling through a gap rather than the job crashing outright.

I'd confirm it cheaply -- line up the missing files' timestamps against the lifecycle cutoff and the cluster's restart schedule, and check the storage account's delete activity around those dates. The fix has two parts, and I'd insist on both: exclude the checkpoint (and schema location) from any lifecycle policy going forward, since those paths need to live indefinitely, and then actually backfill the specific files that already fell through the gap -- restarting the stream won't retroactively pick them up, because whatever high-water mark it's working from has already moved past them. A scoped batch read with modifiedAfter/modifiedBefore into the same table handles that backfill cleanly.
questions.example:
# Backfill the gap window without disturbing the live checkpoint
df = (spark.read.format("cloudFiles")
      .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
      .option("modifiedAfter", "2026-08-15T00:00:00Z")
      .option("modifiedBefore", "2026-09-26T00:00:00Z")
      .load("abfss://source@acct.dfs.core.windows.net/events/"))
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("events.landing")

# Exclude the checkpoint path from the account-wide lifecycle rule
az storage account management-policy show --account-name acct \
  --resource-group rg-data | grep -A5 checkpoints
commonMistakes: Assuming any Autoloader gap must be a malformed/bad-records issue, since that's the well-documented, loud failure mode
Not realizing the checkpoint location holds Autoloader's own file-tracking state, not just Spark's standard offset/commit logs
Applying a lifecycle/retention policy account-wide without excluding checkpoint and schema-tracking paths
Restarting the stream and assuming it will automatically catch up on the already-missed files
Fixing the lifecycle policy going forward but never backfilling the files that were already skipped
keyPoints: Autoloader's checkpoint path holds both standard Structured Streaming offset/commit logs and Autoloader's own RocksDB-backed file-tracking state
Checkpoint and state files are not safe to age out under a blanket lifecycle policy; they must be explicitly excluded
An auto-terminating cluster that reloads state on every run makes this failure mode worse
Diagnosis: correlate missing-file timestamps against the lifecycle cutoff and the cluster-restart cadence, plus storage delete logs
Fix requires excluding the checkpoint path AND a manual backfill -- restarting the stream alone will not recover already-missed files

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Rules out malformed/bad-records as the cause with a specific reason
Correctly explains what state actually lives in the checkpoint beyond standard offsets
Explains the mechanism by which lifecycle deletion causes silent skipping rather than a crash
Proposes excluding the checkpoint path from the lifecycle policy
Proposes a concrete backfill approach for the already-missed files
Proposes ongoing verification/monitoring to catch this earlier next time

questions.title: Notebooks Break With Permission Denied After a Hive Metastore to Unity Catalog Migration
questions.prompt: A team migrated about 40 tables from the legacy Hive metastore into a new Unity Catalog catalog as UC managed tables. The tables show up fine in Catalog Explorer, but the same analysts who ran these notebooks daily for over a year now hit 'PERMISSION_DENIED: User does not have SELECT on Table' errors, even though nobody changed their workspace-level permissions. Walk through why this is happening and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first thing I'd separate out is that an object being visible in Catalog Explorer and a user having an actual grant on it are two completely independent facts in Unity Catalog. Being able to browse the object, or even having successfully queried the old Hive metastore version of it for a year, says nothing about UC privileges on the new object.

The real root cause is that the two access models are fundamentally different. The legacy Hive metastore, depending on how the workspace was configured, typically governed access either through cluster-level settings (on a no-isolation-shared cluster, effectively 'if you can attach to the cluster, you can read the table') or through workspace-local table ACL grants scoped only to that one workspace's metastore. Unity Catalog replaces that entirely with a centralized, deny-by-default, three-level privilege model across catalog, schema, and table. Migrating or cloning the data into a UC managed table creates the object, but it does not carry over any of the old access signals -- there is no automatic inheritance from 'this group could read it before.'

Specifically, for a user to successfully query a UC table they need, at minimum, USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, and SELECT on the table itself (directly or via group membership) -- all three are required, not just one. A very common migration gap is granting SELECT at the table level and forgetting USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, which still blocks access with an equally final-looking permission error.

To diagnose precisely what's missing, I'd run SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG <catalog>, SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA <catalog>.<schema>, and SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE <catalog>.<schema>.<table> for the affected group, and compare that against what the group had on the legacy hive_metastore catalog if table ACLs were enabled there, to understand the expected mapping that never got re-created in UC.

The fix is granting the missing privileges, ideally to a group rather than to individual users: GRANT USE CATALOG, GRANT USE SCHEMA, and GRANT SELECT at the appropriate level. After granting, I'd re-test as an affected user and document the catalog's grant structure so the next migrated batch of tables inherits the same group-level grants automatically rather than requiring another one-off sweep. I'd also double-check that the compute these notebooks run on is attached in a UC-enabled access mode (shared or single-user), since a legacy no-isolation cluster predating UC is a second, less common contributor to the same symptom, though the missing grants are almost always the primary cause here.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The thing I'd point out immediately is that 'the table shows up fine in Catalog Explorer' and 'this user has a grant on it' are two completely unrelated facts in Unity Catalog, and it's an easy trap to conflate them because in the old Hive metastore world, access was often much looser -- tied to cluster config or workspace-local ACLs -- so people are used to 'I can see it, therefore I can query it.' UC doesn't work that way at all; it's deny-by-default, centrally managed, and none of that old access history carries over just because the data got migrated.

What I'd actually check is whether the migration populated any grants at all, because moving the data into a UC managed table and setting up the GRANT structure are two separate steps -- nothing automatic bridges them. And there's a specific trap people fall into even when they do remember to grant something: querying a UC table needs USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, AND SELECT on the table -- all three. Grant just the SELECT and skip the other two, and users still get blocked, just with a slightly different error.

So diagnostically, I'd run SHOW GRANTS at all three levels for the affected catalog, schema, and table, and that'll show me exactly which of the three is missing. The fix is just the missing GRANT statements, but I'd push to grant them to the group, not each user individually, specifically because this exact scenario -- a migration that quietly forgot to port over the access model -- is going to happen again on the next batch of tables if the pattern isn't fixed at the group level. I'd also sanity-check that the cluster people are running these notebooks on is actually in a UC-enabled access mode, since that's a second, less common way the same symptom shows up, but the grant gap is almost always what's actually going on.
commonMistakes: Assuming visibility in Catalog Explorer means the user already has a grant
Granting SELECT on the table but forgetting USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, which still blocks access
Expecting Hive metastore table ACLs or cluster-based access to carry over automatically during migration
Granting individually to users instead of to groups, creating a repeating migration gap
Not checking whether the compute cluster itself is running in a UC-enabled access mode
keyPoints: UC uses a deny-by-default, three-level privilege model (catalog, schema, table) with no automatic inheritance from legacy Hive metastore ACLs
Visibility in Catalog Explorer is independent from actually having a grant
A working query needs USE CATALOG + USE SCHEMA + SELECT, not just one of the three
SHOW GRANTS at each level is the right diagnostic tool to find exactly what's missing
Grant to groups, not individual users, to avoid repeating this gap on every migration batch

Mentions group-based grants and/or compute access-mode as good practice

questions.title: A Fabric Capacity Throttles Every Morning When Business Users Arrive
questions.prompt: An F64 Fabric capacity hosts a workspace with several Direct Lake semantic models and a handful of Dataflow Gen2 refreshes. Starting a few weeks ago, between roughly 9 and 11 AM every weekday, Direct Lake report queries start timing out and new Dataflow Gen2 refreshes get rejected or delayed, even though nothing about the data volumes or report designs has changed recently. By early afternoon everything is fine again. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start in the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app rather than guessing from symptoms, since it's purpose-built to show per-capacity CU (capacity unit) consumption over time, broken out by interactive versus background operations, and to show throttling state directly.

I'd look at the utilization timeline specifically for the 9-11AM window across several days to confirm a reproducible pattern rather than a one-off spike, and check whether consumption is crossing 100% of the capacity's CU allocation specifically during that window, which is what triggers Fabric's throttling policy.

I'd be precise about the mechanism: Fabric capacities use a bursting and smoothing model -- short bursts above 100% are normally absorbed by borrowing against future capacity, but sustained overconsumption accumulates as carry-forward debt, which moves the capacity through throttling stages (an initial delay stage affecting interactive operations, progressively more severe delays, and eventually rejection of new operations) until the debt is worked off during quieter periods. A capacity that's 'fine by early afternoon' is consistent with it paying down accumulated overage once the morning load subsides.

To find what's actually driving the spike, I'd break down consumption by item/operation in the Metrics app during the window. The likely finding is that scheduled Dataflow Gen2 refreshes (and possibly other scheduled jobs) are scheduled right at or near 9 AM -- exactly when interactive Direct Lake query load from arriving business users also peaks -- and the two together push total CU consumption over the capacity, not either one alone.

Given that, I'd sequence the fix from cheapest to most disruptive: first, reschedule the Dataflow Gen2 refreshes (and any other heavy background jobs) outside the 9-11AM window, since that costs nothing and takes effect immediately. If interactive load alone is still enough to saturate the capacity even without competing background jobs, that points to genuine undersizing for the active user count, and the fix is scaling to a larger SKU or splitting background/ETL workloads onto a separate capacity so a batch spike never competes with interactive BI traffic for the same CU pool.

I'd verify by re-checking the Metrics app for the same morning window over several subsequent days to confirm utilization stays under the throttling threshold and that timeouts/rejections stop recurring, rather than declaring victory after a single good morning.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't start by second-guessing the Direct Lake model or the dataflow design -- I'd start in the Fabric Capacity Metrics app, because that's the one place purpose-built to show me CU consumption over time for this specific capacity, split out by interactive versus background load, and it'll tell me directly whether this is a throttling event rather than something else entirely.

What I'm expecting to see, given the 9-11AM pattern repeating every weekday, is utilization crossing 100% specifically in that window. And I'd want to be precise about what that actually means mechanically -- Fabric capacities tolerate short bursts above 100% through a smoothing model, so a brief spike isn't automatically a problem. It's sustained overconsumption that builds up carry-forward debt and triggers the throttling stages -- first slower interactive operations, then more aggressive delays, eventually rejections -- and that debt gets worked off during quieter hours, which lines up perfectly with 'fine again by early afternoon.'

The next thing I'd do inside the Metrics app is break the 9-11AM consumption down by item, because my strong suspicion is that this isn't purely 'too many users logged in' -- it's that scheduled background work, specifically the Dataflow Gen2 refreshes, is scheduled right into the same window as peak interactive login traffic, and the two are stacking on top of each other against one shared CU pool.

If that's confirmed, the cheapest fix is just moving those refreshes to a quieter part of the day -- free, immediate, no infrastructure change. If interactive load alone is still enough to saturate the capacity even with the background jobs moved, that's a genuine sizing problem, and I'd scale to a larger SKU or split background workloads onto a separate capacity so they stop competing for the same pool. Either way, I wouldn't call it fixed off one good morning -- I'd watch the Metrics app across several subsequent days before considering this closed.
questions.example:
Capacity Metrics app checklist:
1. Gauge view: utilization % for the capacity, 9-11AM window, last 7 weekdays
2. Timepoint drill-in: break down CU seconds by item (semantic model refresh, Dataflow Gen2 refresh, report query)
3. Check for overlapping schedules:
   - Dataflow Gen2 refresh schedule: 09:00 daily
   - Peak interactive query load: ~09:00-10:30 daily
4. Fix: move refresh schedule to 06:00, or scale F64 -> F128, or isolate ETL on a second capacity

Not using the Capacity Metrics app and instead guessing from user complaints alone
Treating a short burst over 100% as the problem, missing that sustained carry-forward debt is what actually triggers throttling
Jumping straight to a larger SKU without first checking whether rescheduling competing background jobs would resolve it for free
Declaring victory after a single good morning instead of verifying across several subsequent days

Fabric's bursting/smoothing model throttles on sustained carry-forward overage, not brief bursts
Overlap between scheduled background jobs (Dataflow Gen2 refreshes) and interactive peak usage is the likely driver

questions.title: A Real-Time KQL Dashboard Undercounts Events Versus the Batch Reconciliation Report
questions.prompt: A Fabric Eventstream feeds a KQL database that materializes a per-hour event-count aggregation via an update policy. A nightly batch job reconciles the same source against a landed copy of the raw events and always finds slightly more events than the real-time KQL counts for the matching hour -- the gap is small, under 1%, but persistent, and it is always the KQL side that's lower, never higher. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd first confirm this is actually an out-of-order/lateness issue rather than something like a dedup bug or two pipelines reading different sources. I'd pull the specific event IDs that are missing from the real-time count but present in the batch reconciliation, and compare two timestamps for each: their event-time, and their ingestion_time() into the KQL database. If the missing rows cluster right at hour boundaries and show a consistent lag between event-time and ingestion-time, that confirms late arrival as the mechanism rather than assuming it.

The mechanism itself: a windowed aggregation (hourly bucket keyed on event-time) computed via a KQL update policy has to decide at some point that a window is 'closed' and finalize its aggregate -- it cannot wait indefinitely for stragglers. Any event whose event-time falls inside an hour but which physically arrives after that hour's window has already been sealed gets permanently excluded from the real-time aggregate. The batch reconciliation doesn't have this problem, because by the time it runs that night, there's no ambiguity about whether more data is still coming -- everything has already landed in the raw copy. That explains both the direction of the gap (KQL always lower, never higher) and its small, steady size (only the consistent tail of late-arriving events per hour).

Once lateness is confirmed as the mechanism, the specific thing to check is the Eventstream windowing/aggregation operator's out-of-order/lateness tolerance -- how far past the window's nominal end it will still accept events before sealing it -- compared against the typical event-time-to-ingestion-time lag measured empirically in the first step.

The fix is widening that tolerance to comfortably exceed the observed worst-case arrival jitter, with margin. If the source's lateness is unavoidably large or variable, I'd also consider whether the real-time aggregate should be a revisable materialized view that can update a recently-sealed hour within a bounded grace period, rather than a strictly one-shot seal, so it can self-correct instead of permanently losing the tail.

I'd verify by re-running the same per-hour comparison against the batch reconciliation over several subsequent days to confirm the gap closes to zero, and I'd flag that widening the tolerance only fixes things going forward -- already-sealed historical hours remain under-counted unless a one-time backfill is also run against them.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before I even think about windowing configuration, I'd want hard evidence that this is actually a lateness issue and not something like a dedup bug or two pipelines reading different sources. So I'd pull a handful of the specific events that are missing from the real-time count but present in the batch reconciliation, and look at two timestamps for each: their actual event-time, and their ingestion_time() into the KQL database. If those missing events cluster right at hour boundaries and consistently show meaningful lag between event-time and arrival, that's the mechanism confirmed, not assumed.

The reason that pattern produces exactly this symptom -- small, persistent, always in the same direction -- comes down to how a windowed aggregate has to behave. At some point it has to seal an hour's bucket and finalize a count, because it can't wait forever for stragglers. Anything that arrives event-time-stamped into that hour but physically shows up after the window's already sealed just never makes it into that aggregate -- permanently. The batch job doesn't have that problem at all, because by the time it runs, there's no ambiguity about whether more data is still coming; everything's already landed. That's why the real-time side is always the one that's lower, never the other way around, and why it's a small, steady gap rather than something erratic.

Given that, the actual lever to check is the lateness/out-of-order tolerance configured on the Eventstream windowing step -- specifically whether it's narrower than the real arrival jitter I just measured empirically in the first step. The fix is to widen that tolerance with some margin above the observed worst case, or, if the source's lateness is genuinely large and variable, move toward an aggregate that can still revise a recently-sealed window for a bounded grace period instead of treating sealing as final.

And I'd be upfront that widening the tolerance only fixes things going forward -- it doesn't retroactively fill in hours that already sealed under the old, too-narrow setting, so I'd check whether those need a one-time backfill too.

Not checking the specific missing records' event-time vs. ingestion-time, so never actually confirming lateness as the mechanism
Widening KQL retention or ingestion batching settings instead of the actual windowing lateness tolerance on the aggregation step
Treating the gap as acceptable 'real-time is just approximate' without quantifying whether it's bounded, recurring lateness versus unbounded data loss
Fixing the tolerance going forward but not backfilling already-sealed historical windows that remain permanently under-counted
keyPoints: Confirm the mechanism empirically: missing-event event-time vs. ingestion-time gap clustered at hour boundaries
A sealed windowed aggregate permanently drops events that arrive after its lateness tolerance, while a batch job always catches up
A one-directional, small, persistent gap is the signature of a too-narrow out-of-order/lateness tolerance, not data loss
Fix: widen the windowing step's lateness tolerance to exceed observed real-world arrival jitter
Verify against the batch reconciliation over multiple days after the change, and backfill already-sealed hours separately

Correctly explains why a sealed windowed aggregate permanently drops late events while batch doesn't

Proposes widening tolerance (and/or a revisable aggregate) as the fix
Verifies against batch reconciliation and addresses already-sealed historical windows

questions.title: A Kafka Consumer Group Keeps Rebalancing Even Though Nothing Is Crashing
questions.prompt: A latency-sensitive consumer group reads from a 12-partition topic and writes each record to a downstream store. Over the last couple of weeks the group has started logging repeated rebalances every few minutes under completely normal load -- no consumer processes are crashing or restarting, there are no OOMs, and CPU/memory look fine -- but end-to-end latency has been creeping upward over the same period. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd pull the actual broker-side and client-side logs around a rebalance event first, rather than guessing from symptoms. The specific thing to look for is the group coordinator's stated reason for removing a member -- a log line referencing the consumer exceeding its poll interval versus one referencing a heartbeat/session failure. That phrasing specifically identifies which of two separate Kafka timers is firing.

The reason 'rebalancing but nothing's crashing' is a specific, well-known pattern: since KIP-62, Kafka decoupled heartbeating from the application's poll loop by running heartbeats on a background thread. That means session.timeout.ms, which governs heartbeat-based liveness, can be perfectly healthy -- the process looks completely alive to the coordinator -- while a separate timer, max.poll.interval.ms, governs how long the consumer is allowed to go between calls to poll() while it's busy processing the records from the previous poll. If processing the downstream write takes too long, the consumer never gets back to poll() in time, the coordinator assumes it's stuck, and triggers a rebalance -- all while the process itself is alive, healthy, and heartbeating normally.

I'd treat 'latency has been creeping upward' as the same root cause as the rebalances, not a separate symptom. Something in the downstream write path -- the datastore, a dependency call, connection pool saturation, growing batch sizes -- has been getting slower over these same weeks, and as average per-poll processing time crept closer to and then past max.poll.interval.ms, rebalances started appearing. I'd pull metrics for the downstream write path directly and correlate its latency trend against the timestamps of the rebalance events to confirm the timeline lines up.

I'd also check max.poll.records and the consumer's actual observed per-poll processing time if instrumented: a large max.poll.records pulls a bigger batch per poll, which multiplies the effect of any per-record slowdown into a larger total processing time, making it more likely to blow through max.poll.interval.ms even from a modest per-record regression.

The fix, roughly in priority order: fix the actual downstream slowdown first, since that's the real regression (e.g., fix the slow dependency, add concurrency/backpressure rather than one-record-at-a-time synchronous writes); reduce max.poll.records so each poll's batch is faster to fully process; and, as a stop-gap only, increase max.poll.interval.ms to add headroom while the underlying slowdown is being addressed. A more durable architectural fix is decoupling consumption from processing with an internal bounded queue/thread pool so poll() can keep returning promptly even while a backlog of writes is being worked through. I'd verify by confirming rebalance events stop appearing in the logs and that observed per-poll processing time comfortably stays under max.poll.interval.ms with margin, not just barely under it.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The detail that jumps out at me immediately is 'rebalancing but nothing's crashing' -- because that combination almost always means people are mentally merging two Kafka timers that are actually completely separate since KIP-62. session.timeout.ms governs heartbeats, and heartbeats run on their own background thread now, independent of whatever the application thread is doing. So a consumer can be heartbeating perfectly healthily -- looking completely alive to the coordinator -- while still getting kicked out of the group for a totally different reason: taking too long between calls to poll(), which is what max.poll.interval.ms actually governs.

So I wouldn't go looking for crash logs at all. I'd go straight to the coordinator's log line explaining why it removed the member, and I'd expect to see language specifically about exceeding the poll interval, not a heartbeat failure -- that's the piece of evidence that tells me definitively which of the two timers is actually firing.

And I wouldn't treat the rebalancing and the creeping latency as two separate problems to investigate -- they're the same problem. Something downstream, wherever these records are being written, has been getting slower over these same weeks, and as the time spent processing each batch crept up toward max.poll.interval.ms, it eventually started crossing it. I'd go look at whatever write path these records hit -- the datastore, a dependency call, connection pool health -- and line its latency trend up against when the rebalances started.

I'd also check max.poll.records, because that's the multiplier here: if the consumer's pulling a big batch per poll, a modest per-record slowdown gets magnified into a much bigger total processing time, which makes blowing through the poll interval way more likely. My actual fix is to go fix whatever's slow downstream first, since that's the real regression; shrinking max.poll.records and maybe decoupling consumption from processing with an internal queue are good supporting changes, but just cranking up max.poll.interval.ms on its own would only be masking a regression that's still getting worse.
questions.example:
# Broker/coordinator log line to look for (the deciding evidence):
# "Member consumer-3-abc... sending LeaveGroup because member is removed from the consumer group:
#  consumer poll timeout has expired." -> max.poll.interval.ms issue, NOT a heartbeat/session failure

# Relevant config to inspect / adjust:
# max.poll.interval.ms = 300000   (default; raise only as a stop-gap)
# max.poll.records     = 500      (lower to reduce per-poll processing time)
# session.timeout.ms   = 10000    (separate timer -- not the cause here)

Confusing session.timeout.ms (heartbeat liveness) with max.poll.interval.ms (poll-loop processing budget) -- separate timers since KIP-62
Fixing it by only raising max.poll.interval.ms without addressing the actual downstream slowdown causing the creep
Not checking max.poll.records, missing that a large batch size amplifies a modest per-record slowdown into a poll-interval violation
Processing records synchronously one-by-one inside the poll loop instead of decoupling consumption from processing
keyPoints: The specific coordinator log line for a poll-interval-based removal is the deciding diagnostic evidence
session.timeout.ms (heartbeat thread) and max.poll.interval.ms (poll-loop processing budget) are decoupled since KIP-62 and fail independently
Creeping end-to-end latency is the same root cause as the rebalances, not a separate symptom
max.poll.records amplifies the effect of a per-record slowdown on the poll-interval budget
Fix the actual downstream slowdown; use max.poll.records/max.poll.interval.ms and decoupled processing as supporting changes, not the whole fix

Identifies the correct diagnostic log evidence (poll-timeout removal, not a liveness failure)
Connects the creeping latency to the rebalance root cause

Proposes fixing the downstream slowdown plus appropriate config/architecture changes

questions.title: A Kafka Connect Sink to Postgres Has Been Silently Dropping Records for Weeks
questions.prompt: A JDBC sink connector writes events from a Kafka topic into a downstream Postgres table. The connector has been running for weeks with a healthy RUNNING status and no task failures, but a reconciliation job comparing topic offsets consumed against rows written shows a small, recurring gap -- roughly a few records a day are simply missing from Postgres, with nothing in the connector logs at the default log level calling out an error. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and the fix, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd start from what the healthy RUNNING status with zero task failures actually tells me. Kafka Connect's default error-handling mode, errors.tolerance=none, kills the task outright on the very first bad record it hits during conversion, transformation, or the sink write -- the task would show FAILED in the Connect REST API, not RUNNING. The fact that it's stayed healthy for weeks despite records clearly going missing is itself strong evidence that errors.tolerance=all has already been set on this connector, likely specifically so it wouldn't die on occasional malformed records -- which changes the failure behavior from 'stop everything' to 'skip the bad record and keep going.'

I'd confirm that directly rather than infer it: pull the connector's config via the Connect REST API (GET /connectors/<name>/config) and check errors.tolerance, and specifically whether errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name is set.

The actual gap in the design is that errors.tolerance=all on its own only prevents the task from dying -- it does not, by itself, preserve the records that failed. Unless a dead-letter-queue topic is explicitly configured, a record that fails conversion, transformation, or the sink write itself (e.g., a type mismatch against a Postgres column, a constraint violation, a null in a NOT NULL column) is simply skipped, and the per-record failure shows up only as an error-count metric and typically a WARN-level log line -- easy to miss at the default INFO logging level, which matches exactly what's described here.

To find the specific failing records, I'd temporarily raise log verbosity for the relevant connector classes (or check whatever metrics/JMX endpoint exposes sink task error counters), and replay a known missing offset through a throwaway consumer to see precisely what the JDBC sink chokes on.

The fix is configuring a dead-letter-queue topic for the connector (errors.tolerance=all, errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name=<dlq-topic>, with an appropriate replication factor and errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true for useful metadata) so future skipped records are preserved and inspectable rather than vanishing. Separately, I'd fix the underlying data-quality issue causing the skips if it's addressable upstream (a schema/validation fix or a sanitizing transform before the sink). I'd be explicit that this doesn't recover what's already been lost -- those records were never captured anywhere, so recovering them means replaying from the source topic by offset if retention still covers that range, or accepting the historical gap and backfilling from another source of truth. I'd verify by confirming a deliberately bad test record lands in the DLQ topic instead of disappearing, and by re-running the reconciliation job going forward to confirm the gap stops growing.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd say out loud here is: a healthy, never-failed RUNNING connector tells me nothing about whether records are getting lost, and that's actually the whole clue. Kafka Connect's default behavior, errors.tolerance=none, would have killed this task the very first time it hit a bad record -- it would be sitting there FAILED in the Connect REST API, not quietly RUNNING for weeks. The fact that it's still up means somebody already changed that setting, almost certainly specifically to stop it from dying on occasional bad data, and that change is what opened the door to silent loss.

I'd confirm that directly rather than guess -- pull the connector's config from the REST API and check errors.tolerance and whether a dead-letter-queue topic is configured. My expectation is errors.tolerance=all with no DLQ topic set, and if that's the case, the behavior makes complete sense: tolerance=all only stops the task from dying on a bad record, it doesn't do anything to preserve that record. Without a DLQ configured, a record that fails conversion or the actual write to Postgres -- say, a type mismatch or a constraint violation -- just gets skipped, with the only trace being an error counter and maybe a WARN-level log line, which is easy to miss if the operational logging is set at INFO, exactly matching 'nothing in the logs at default level.'

Once I've got that confirmed, I'd want to actually see which records are failing and why -- bump log verbosity or check the error metrics, and replay one of the specific missing offsets through a throwaway consumer to see exactly what the JDBC sink chokes on.

The fix is adding a dead-letter-queue topic to the connector config so future failures land somewhere inspectable instead of vanishing, plus actually fixing whatever data-quality issue is causing the failures in the first place. And I'd flag clearly that this doesn't recover what's already been lost -- those records were never captured anywhere, so that's a separate conversation about whether they can be replayed from source retention or just have to be accepted as a historical gap.
commonMistakes: Assuming a healthy RUNNING connector with no task failures rules out data loss
Not realizing errors.tolerance=all without a configured DLQ means failed records are silently dropped, not retried or preserved
Looking only at default INFO-level logs and concluding there's no evidence, without checking error metrics or raising log verbosity
Fixing the connector config going forward but not accounting for the already-lost historical records
Assuming the issue must be Postgres-side (a trigger or constraint silently rejecting rows) before checking the Connect error-handling configuration
keyPoints: A healthy RUNNING status with errors.tolerance=all tells you nothing about whether records are being silently skipped
errors.tolerance=all alone doesn't preserve failed records -- it just stops the task from dying; a DLQ topic is what actually preserves them
Skipped-record evidence lives in WARN-level logs and error-count metrics, easy to miss at default INFO logging
Fix: configure a dead-letter-queue topic and investigate the specific records' failure reason
Historical already-dropped records need a separate backfill/replay plan since they were never captured anywhere

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why RUNNING status is compatible with ongoing silent data loss
Identifies errors.tolerance=all without a DLQ as the specific mechanism
Proposes a concrete way to find the specific failing records (metrics/logs/replay)
Proposes configuring a DLQ topic as the fix
Addresses the already-lost historical records separately

questions.title: Terraform Apply Fails With 'Resource Already Exists' After a Manual Incident Fix
questions.prompt: During an incident last week, an engineer manually created a storage account and a couple of firewall rules directly in the Azure Portal to restore service quickly, without updating the Terraform code or state for the shared data-platform environment. Nobody has touched the Terraform configuration for those resources since. Today's terraform apply for that environment fails with Azure errors that the storage account and firewall rules already exist. Walk through how you'd diagnose this and safely bring Terraform back in sync, in the order you'd actually do it.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd read the actual error carefully first: an Azure 'already exists' or conflict error on an apply, for a resource that terraform plan showed as 'will be created' rather than 'will be updated,' is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change -- the real resource exists in Azure, but Terraform's state has no record of it, so Terraform tries to create it from scratch and Azure's own uniqueness constraints reject the duplicate.

I'd confirm the drift explicitly rather than assume it: run terraform plan and verify the affected resources show as '+ create,' and cross-reference the resource names/IDs from the error against what's actually visible via az resource show or the Portal. In this case that directly confirms the incident-week manual resources are the cause.

Structurally, this happens because Terraform state is only ever updated by Terraform itself -- through apply, import, or refresh. Any resource created directly through the Portal, the CLI, or by an engineer bypassing Terraform is completely invisible to the state file no matter how long it's existed, and a plan has no way to discover it on its own; it only compares the configuration against what's already recorded in state.

The fix is terraform import. For each drifted resource, I'd get its real Azure resource ID (az resource show --name ... --resource-group ... --resource-type ... --query id) and run terraform import <resource_address_in_config> <azure_resource_id> to attach the real object into state under the matching address. This requires a resource block already existing in the .tf configuration for that address -- import only binds state, it doesn't generate configuration, unless using Terraform's newer import block with -generate-config-out, which can scaffold a starting config from the real resource if the .tf code doesn't exist yet.

After importing, I'd immediately run terraform plan again -- this is the step people skip. Import only syncs the state's existence record; it says nothing about whether the .tf configuration's attributes actually match what was configured manually during the incident (for example, a firewall rule's IP range might differ from what's in code). The follow-up plan will show any genuine attribute drift as an '~ update,' which has to be reconciled deliberately: either update the .tf code to match the real, intentional incident configuration, or apply to bring the resource back to the originally-intended configuration, depending on which is actually correct going forward.

Beyond the immediate fix, I'd treat this as a process signal: if manual changes during an incident are sometimes unavoidable, build a habit or runbook step of importing them back into Terraform (or at minimum filing a ticket to do so) right after the incident closes, rather than discovering the drift weeks later at the next unrelated apply.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The error message itself tells me almost everything before I look at anything else -- Azure saying a resource 'already exists' on something Terraform's plan wanted to create, not update, is basically the textbook signature of state drift. Something real exists out there that Terraform's state file has simply never heard of.

I wouldn't just assume that, though -- I'd run plan and actually look at whether it's showing a '+ create' for those resources, and cross-check the names against what's genuinely sitting in the Portal or az resource show. In this case that's trivial to confirm, because we already know exactly what happened: someone created these by hand in the Portal during last week's incident, and nothing about that touched Terraform's code or state.

The mechanical reason this happens is worth being precise about: Terraform's state file only ever gets updated by Terraform itself. It has no way to notice, on its own, that a human created something matching its configuration out-of-band -- it just compares its config against whatever it already has on record, and if there's no record, its only option is to try to create it, which collides with the real one that's already there.

So the fix is terraform import -- get the real Azure resource ID, point it at the matching resource address in the .tf config, and import binds the two together in state. The part I'd be careful not to skip is what comes right after: import only fixes the fact that Terraform now knows the resource exists. It says nothing about whether the configuration in code actually matches what got configured by hand during the incident. So the very next thing is another plan, and whatever shows up as an update this time -- maybe a firewall rule's IP range doesn't match -- is a deliberate decision to make: update the code to reflect the real, intentional incident fix, or apply to bring it back to what was originally intended. Either is fine, but it has to be a decision, not an accident. And longer-term, I'd push for a habit of importing incident-time manual changes back into Terraform right away, rather than discovering this kind of drift at the next unrelated apply weeks later.
questions.example:
# Get the real Azure resource ID
az storage account show --name stdataplat01 --resource-group rg-data-platform --query id -o tsv

# Bind it into state at the matching config address
terraform import azurerm_storage_account.data_platform \
  /subscriptions/xxxx/resourceGroups/rg-data-platform/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stdataplat01

# ALWAYS re-plan after import to catch attribute-level drift
terraform plan

Deleting the manually-created Azure resources to let Terraform recreate them cleanly, discarding the incident fix
Running terraform import without first confirming via plan which specific resources/attributes are actually drifted
Treating import as a complete fix and not re-running plan afterward to catch attribute-level drift
Importing into the wrong resource address, not matching an existing/correct resource block, causing a different drift
keyPoints: 'Already exists' on a planned create, not an update, is the specific signature of state drift from an out-of-band change
Terraform state only changes via Terraform itself; manually-created resources are invisible to it until explicitly imported
terraform import attaches an existing real resource to a state address but requires a matching config block (or the import block with -generate-config-out)
Import only fixes existence tracking -- a follow-up plan is required to catch and reconcile attribute-level drift
Process takeaway: import out-of-band incident changes back into Terraform promptly, not weeks later

Explains why Terraform state doesn't auto-discover manually created resources
Walks through terraform import correctly (resource ID lookup, address, requires config)
Emphasizes re-running plan after import to catch attribute drift
Notes a process improvement for future incidents

questions.title: A Stuck Terraform State Lock Is Blocking Every Deployment After a CI Crash
questions.prompt: A CI pipeline running terraform apply against a remote state backend lost network connectivity partway through and the job was killed before it could finish. Every terraform apply, and even terraform plan, run against that environment since has failed immediately with a state lock error, and the team is blocked from deploying anything to that environment. Walk through how you'd safely diagnose and resolve this, in the order you'd actually do it, including what you'd check before touching the lock.
questions.modelAnswer:
I'd read the lock error output carefully first. Most backends that support locking (Azure Storage via a blob lease, S3 with a DynamoDB lock table, Terraform Cloud) surface identifying details directly in the error -- a Lock ID, who or what acquired it, and a timestamp. That information is the starting point, not something to skip past to get straight to unlocking.

Before touching anything, I'd rule out that this is a real, currently-in-progress apply rather than a stale lock left behind by the crashed job. I'd check the CI system's own run history or dashboard for that environment to confirm no other pipeline run is actively executing right now, and if there's any ambiguity I'd check with the team or on-call directly. The entire point of the lock is to prevent two concurrent applies from reading and writing the shared state file at the same time, which can corrupt it -- one apply's changes getting silently overwritten by the other's stale read is the real danger here, not a hypothetical one, so removing a lock that's protecting a genuinely active apply is the actual risk I'm managing against.

Once I've confirmed no other apply is running, I'd check whether the underlying state storage itself was left in a bad condition by the crash, not just locked -- for an Azure Storage backend, checking the blob's lease status directly (az storage blob show), and checking whether blob soft-delete or versioning is enabled so I could inspect or recover a prior good version of the state file if needed. For other backends I'd check the equivalent, such as a DynamoDB lock table item for S3, or the run status in Terraform Cloud.

To resolve the stale lock itself, I'd run terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> using the Lock ID from the error message. This only removes the lock record; it doesn't touch or validate the actual state file contents.

Immediately afterward I'd verify state integrity before trusting it: run terraform plan and read it carefully. If the crashed apply got partway through actually changing real infrastructure before losing connectivity, the state file may not fully reflect that, and the plan might show unexpected diffs for resources that were mid-change. I'd compare anything surprising against what's actually deployed (az resource show or the Portal) before applying further, and if the state looks meaningfully inconsistent with reality, I'd consider reconciling it or, in the worst case, pulling a previous good state version from backend versioning rather than trusting a possibly-partial write.

Once plan looks sane, I'd proceed with a normal apply. As a process follow-up, I'd flag whether the CI pipeline needs better handling for interrupted runs -- a cleanup step, or relying on the backend's native lease/lock timeout where supported -- so an infrastructure blip doesn't require a manual force-unlock every time.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Before I touch the lock at all, I want to understand what it's actually there to prevent, because that framing changes how carefully I approach this. The lock exists so two applies can't read and write the same state file at the same time -- if that happened, one apply's changes could silently get clobbered by the other's stale read, which is a much worse problem than being temporarily blocked. So my first move isn't force-unlock, it's making sure I'm not about to remove a lock that's protecting something that's genuinely still running.

I'd check the CI system's own history for that environment to confirm nothing is actively executing, and if there's any doubt, I'd just ask the team directly rather than guess. Once I'm confident the lock is stale -- left behind by the job that got killed mid-run when it lost connectivity -- I'd look at the lock error itself, which for most backends gives me a Lock ID and some context about who/what acquired it, and I'd also check the underlying storage directly, like the blob's lease status if this is an Azure Storage backend, to see if there's anything else inconsistent beyond just the lock.

Then force-unlock with that specific Lock ID. But I don't treat that as the finish line -- force-unlock only removes the lock record, it doesn't tell me anything about whether the state file itself is trustworthy after a crash that happened mid-apply. So the very next thing is a plan, read carefully: if the crashed run had actually started changing real infrastructure before it lost connectivity, the state might not fully reflect that, and I'd expect to see it in unexpected diffs. If anything looks off, I'd rather pull a known-good prior version of the state from the backend's versioning than apply on top of something I don't trust. Only once plan looks sane do I let anyone apply again, and I'd flag the CI pipeline's handling of interrupted runs as a real follow-up so this doesn't become a recurring manual fire drill.
questions.example:
# Error typically includes the Lock ID and holder info:
# Error: Error acquiring the state lock
# Lock Info:
#   ID:        7f3a1c2e-...
#   Operation: OperationTypeApply
#   Who:       ci-runner-42
#   Created:   2026-10-02 09:14:03 UTC

# Confirm no apply is genuinely still running (CI history), then:
az storage blob show --container-name tfstate --name prod.terraform.tfstate --account-name tfstateacct

terraform force-unlock 7f3a1c2e-...

# Verify state integrity before trusting it
terraform plan
commonMistakes: Running terraform force-unlock immediately without first confirming no apply is genuinely still in progress
Treating the lock itself as the problem rather than asking what it's protecting against
Assuming the state file is definitely fine once the lock is removed, without reviewing plan output for signs of a partial write
Not checking whether the crashed apply actually changed real infrastructure before the connection dropped
Manually deleting the lock blob/file instead of using the proper force-unlock command, risking an inconsistent backend locking state
keyPoints: The lock exists to prevent two concurrent applies from corrupting shared state via simultaneous read-modify-write, not as an arbitrary safeguard
Always confirm no apply is genuinely still running before force-unlocking

questions.title: Fixing a SQL-Injectable Dynamic Search Procedure
questions.prompt: A teammate wrote the stored procedure below to let a reporting UI search products by color with a user-selectable sort column. Identify every injection vector in it, then rewrite it safely. Explain specifically why the color value and the sort column name have to be handled differently -- one can be parameterized directly, the other cannot.
questions.modelAnswer:
There are two separate injection vectors here, and they need two different fixes.

The first is @Color: it's concatenated directly into the string inside quotes, so a value like `Red'; DROP TABLE Production.Product; --` gets executed as part of the statement. This is the classic case sp_executesql exists to solve -- @Color is a data value, so it belongs in sp_executesql's parameter list, where SQL Server treats it strictly as data and never as executable text, no matter what characters it contains.

The second is @SortColumn, and it's actually the more dangerous one because it can't be fixed the same way. sp_executesql's parameters only substitute values -- they cannot substitute an identifier like a column name, because `ORDER BY @Param` isn't valid T-SQL (SQL Server would try to sort by a constant, not by a column). That means @SortColumn has to be handled by validation, not parameterization: either whitelist it against a known, fixed list of legal column names before it ever reaches the dynamic string, or at minimum wrap it in QUOTENAME() to neutralize bracket-based injection tricks -- and I'd do both, since QUOTENAME alone doesn't stop someone passing a syntactically valid but unintended column name.

The corrected version below parameterizes @Color through sp_executesql and validates @SortColumn against an explicit allow-list before concatenating it (safely, as an identifier, not a value).
questions.professionalAnswer:
Looking at this procedure, I'd flag it immediately in a code review -- it's building the entire WHERE and ORDER BY clause by gluing strings together, and that's a textbook SQL injection hole. There are actually two different problems stacked on top of each other, and I'd want to be clear they need different fixes. The Color value is a data value, so the right move is sp_executesql with a proper parameter -- that's the whole reason sp_executesql exists, it treats whatever gets passed in purely as data, so even something like a stray apostrophe or an embedded DROP TABLE just becomes a literal string being compared, not code getting executed.

The sort column is trickier, and I'd explain why it can't get the same treatment: you physically cannot parameterize an identifier the way you parameterize a value -- ORDER BY @SomeParam just doesn't do what you'd want, it won't sort by a column, it'll try to sort by whatever that one value is. So for something like a sort column, I always reach for a whitelist -- check the incoming value against the small, fixed list of columns we actually allow sorting by, fall back to a safe default if it's not on the list, and only then build it into the dynamic SQL as an identifier, wrapped in QUOTENAME for good measure.
commonMistakes: Parameterizing only the value and missing that the sort column is a second, separate injection vector
Trying to pass the sort column as an sp_executesql parameter, which doesn't work for identifiers
Relying on QUOTENAME alone for the sort column without an allow-list behind it
Using EXEC() with concatenated strings instead of sp_executesql
Assuming input validation on the UI side is sufficient and skipping server-side protection
keyPoints: sp_executesql parameterizes data values safely; EXEC() with concatenation does not
Identifiers (column/table names) cannot be parameterized -- only values can
Dynamic identifiers must be validated against a whitelist, optionally plus QUOTENAME
Reach for dynamic SQL only when a real identifier or structural element must vary at runtime
SQL injection risk exists even inside stored procedures, not just at the application layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies both injection vectors (value and identifier)
Explains why sp_executesql parameters can't substitute identifiers
Provides a correct, safe rewrite using sp_executesql
Includes identifier whitelisting/QUOTENAME for the sort column
Clear overall explanation of the fix

questions.title: Diagnosing a Recurring Deadlock Between Two Order-Processing Procedures
questions.prompt: Two stored procedures are both involved in order processing: usp_UpdateOrderStatus updates the Orders table first, then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount updates OrderDetails first, then Orders. Under heavy load during a sale event, both start failing intermittently with error 1205. Walk through how you'd confirm this is a genuine deadlock rather than ordinary blocking, what SQL Server already did automatically before you even got paged, how you'd capture the diagnostic evidence, and how you'd redesign the two procedures so this stops recurring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Error 1205 is the giveaway on its own -- it's SQL Server's specific "transaction was deadlocked" error, distinct from ordinary blocking (which doesn't raise an error at all; it just makes the waiting session sit there until the lock is released or the query times out). So the first confirmation is simply that message text and code, not a guess.

Before anyone got paged, SQL Server's lock monitor already detected the cycle automatically and picked one of the two transactions as the deadlock victim, rolling it back on its own and raising 1205 in that session, while letting the other transaction proceed normally. That's expected, automatic behavior -- the problem isn't that SQL Server handled a deadlock; it's that the application design is creating deadlocks in the first place.

To get real evidence instead of guessing, I'd capture the actual deadlock graph: either the system_health Extended Events session (which captures deadlock graphs by default on every modern SQL Server instance with zero setup), or trace flag 1222 writing deadlock graphs to the error log, or a live SQL Server Profiler trace with the Deadlock graph event if I need to reproduce it under controlled load. The graph shows exactly which two sessions were involved, which resources (specific rows/keys/pages) each one held and was waiting on, and which queries were running -- that's what turns "it deadlocks sometimes" into "usp_UpdateOrderStatus held a lock on Orders row X while waiting on OrderDetails row Y, and usp_ApplyDiscount had the exact opposite."

The root cause here is visible just from the procedure descriptions, independent of the graph: the two procedures touch the same two tables in opposite order. usp_UpdateOrderStatus locks Orders then OrderDetails; usp_ApplyDiscount locks OrderDetails then Orders. Under enough concurrent load, it's inevitable that one session grabs the first lock each procedure needs right as the other grabs the second, and neither can proceed. The fix is to enforce a single, consistent access order across every procedure that touches both tables -- rewrite usp_ApplyDiscount to update Orders before OrderDetails, matching usp_UpdateOrderStatus. I'd also shorten both transactions to only what genuinely needs to be atomic, consider whether the default isolation level is adding unnecessary lock duration for this workload, and add application-side retry logic that catches 1205 specifically and retries the transaction once, since even with consistent ordering, some contention under extreme load is still possible.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The first thing I'd point to is that error 1205 is specific -- it's SQL Server's deadlock error, not generic blocking, so I already know what category of problem this is before I even look at the code. And something people sometimes miss: by the time I'm looking at this, SQL Server has already handled the immediate crisis on its own -- it detected the cycle, picked a victim, rolled that one transaction back, and let the other one finish. So I'm not firefighting an active deadlock; I'm investigating why this keeps happening.

To get real evidence I'd go straight to the deadlock graph -- these days that's usually just querying the system_health Extended Events session, since it captures deadlock graphs automatically without me having to turn anything on ahead of time. If I needed something more targeted I'd reach for trace flag 1222 or a Profiler trace with the deadlock graph event. That graph tells me exactly which resources each session was holding and waiting on, which is the proof, not just a theory.

But honestly, in this specific case, I could probably guess the root cause just from the procedure descriptions: one updates Orders then OrderDetails, the other does it backwards. That's the single most common cause of a deadlock -- two pieces of code locking the same two tables in opposite order. My fix is to make every procedure that touches both tables agree on one consistent order, keep the transactions as short as possible so the window for collision is small, and add retry logic around 1205 specifically on the application side as a safety net, since consistent ordering reduces deadlocks dramatically but doesn't mathematically guarantee zero under extreme concurrency.
commonMistakes: Treating ordinary blocking and a deadlock (error 1205) as the same thing
Assuming a deadlock means SQL Server malfunctioned rather than handled an application design flaw
Guessing at the cause instead of capturing the actual deadlock graph
Fixing only the symptom (retrying) without addressing the inconsistent table access order
Wrapping the entire procedure in one long transaction instead of minimizing what's actually atomic
keyPoints: Error 1205 specifically identifies a deadlock, distinct from ordinary blocking
SQL Server automatically detects deadlocks and rolls back a chosen victim
system_health Extended Events / trace flag 1222 / Profiler capture the deadlock graph for real evidence
Root cause here is inconsistent table access order across the two procedures
Fix: enforce consistent access order, keep transactions short, add retry logic for 1205

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes deadlock (1205) from ordinary blocking
Describes SQL Server's automatic deadlock detection and victim rollback
