questions.title: A Combined CI/CD Pipeline for Databricks Code and Terraform Infrastructure
questions.prompt: Design a combined CI/CD pipeline that deploys both Databricks notebook/pipeline changes and the underlying Terraform-managed infrastructure for a data platform together. Walk through ordering -- infra before code or the other way around -- environment promotion, and rollback for each layer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Infra generally has to be in place before the code that depends on it runs -- a job can't use a Unity Catalog schema, a cluster policy, or a secret scope that Terraform hasn't provisioned yet. But that doesn't mean they belong in one lockstep pipeline; it means infra deploys through its own pipeline, on its own cadence (infra changes far less often than notebooks/jobs do), with its own gating -- plan review, policy checks via something like Checkov or tflint, and a required approval for anything touching prod. The code pipeline, packaging notebooks/jobs/pipelines as versioned Databricks Asset Bundles, runs separately and more frequently, and only needs to wait on the infra pipeline when a specific code change actually depends on an infra change that hasn't landed yet.

Both pipelines promote through the same dev -> test/staging -> prod sequence, each with environment-specific configuration -- infra via tfvars per environment, code via DAB's own per-environment target configuration -- and each gated by automated validation appropriate to that layer: infra gets plan review and policy-as-code checks before apply, code gets unit and integration tests run against the dev or staging workspace before promotion. Prod promotion for both layers requires an explicit manual approval, but they're still two separate approvals for two separate changes, not one combined gate that forces every code deploy to also re-approve infra.

Rollback also has to stay decoupled, because conflating the two makes a simple code bug into an infra incident. A bad notebook or job change rolls back by redeploying the previous version of the Databricks Asset Bundle -- since it's a versioned, git-tagged artifact, that's a fast, low-risk redeploy that doesn't touch infrastructure at all. A bad infra change rolls back by reverting to a previous Terraform state/module version and re-applying -- never by manually editing resources in the portal, which breaks the state's accuracy going forward. Keeping these two rollback paths independent is exactly why the pipelines shouldn't be merged into one: the far more common failure mode is a code bug, and you want that fixable in minutes without touching infra at all.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My rule of thumb: infra needs to exist before the code that depends on it runs, but that's a dependency, not a reason to merge the pipelines. Infra gets its own pipeline that runs less often, with stricter gating -- plan review, policy checks, a real approval for prod -- because infra mistakes are expensive and slow to notice. Code -- notebooks, jobs, pipelines packaged as Databricks Asset Bundles -- gets its own pipeline that runs more often, with its own tests, and it only waits on the infra pipeline when a specific change genuinely needs something infra hasn't provisioned yet.

Both go through the same dev -> staging -> prod promotion sequence, each with their own environment-specific config and their own tests appropriate to what they are, and prod for either one needs an actual approval -- but two separate approvals, not one that drags code changes into re-approving infra every time.

Where I'd really push to keep them separate is rollback. If a notebook breaks something, I want to redeploy the previous version of that bundle in minutes and be done -- no infra involved. If an infra change breaks something, that's a Terraform state revert and a careful re-apply, never a manual portal edit that leaves the state lying about reality. Code bugs are the far more common failure, and the whole point of keeping these pipelines decoupled is that fixing one doesn't require touching the other.
commonMistakes: Coupling infra and code into one monolithic pipeline so every code change risks triggering unnecessary infra changes
Giving infra changes the same light-touch approval as routine code deploys instead of stricter gating
Manually applying Terraform for prod instead of running it through a gated pipeline
Having no versioned rollback story for jobs/notebooks, relying on manual redeploy from memory
Not testing infra changes (plan review, policy-as-code) with the same rigor code changes get before promotion
keyPoints: Infra generally deploys ahead of dependent code, but as a separate, less frequent, more strictly gated pipeline
Both layers promote through the same dev -> test -> prod sequence with their own environment-specific configuration
Databricks Asset Bundles version and parameterize code deployments analogous to how Terraform modules version infra
Rollback means redeploying a prior versioned artifact or state, never manual edits
Decoupled pipelines mean a code rollback never requires touching infra, and vice versa

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ordering/dependency reasoning between infra and code pipelines
Correct promotion and environment-gating design for both layers
Mentions Databricks Asset Bundles or an equivalent versioned code deployment mechanism
Correct, decoupled rollback strategy for infra versus code

questions.title: Telling Under-Provisioned Apart From Wasteful When the Databricks + Fabric Bill Spikes
questions.prompt: A data platform's monthly Databricks plus Fabric bill has grown faster than its underlying data volume. Design a cost-optimization approach covering Databricks cluster sizing/autoscaling policy and Fabric capacity right-sizing, and explain exactly how you'd tell the difference between a workload that's genuinely under-provisioned and one that's just wasteful.
questions.modelAnswer:
On the Databricks side, the first structural fix is almost always the cluster type: scheduled production jobs should run on job clusters, which spin up for the job and tear down when it finishes, rather than all-purpose clusters, which bill for the entire time they're running -- idle included -- and are meant for interactive development, not scheduled pipelines. Beyond that, autoscaling with sane min/max worker bounds, auto-termination on any remaining all-purpose clusters, and centrally enforced cluster policies (capping instance types and max DBUs a team can request) close off the common ways individual teams quietly over-provision without anyone noticing until the bill arrives.

On the Fabric side, capacity is a shared pool of Capacity Units across every workload in that capacity -- Lakehouse, Warehouse, Power BI, Real-Time Intelligence -- so right-sizing means watching the Fabric Capacity Metrics app over time rather than guessing at a SKU. Fabric also supports autoscale billing for genuine spikes, which is usually a better fit than permanently provisioning for peak load that only happens occasionally.

The actual diagnostic for under-provisioned versus wasteful is utilization pattern, not the bill. Genuine under-provisioning shows up as sustained high utilization, throttling events, queued background operations, or jobs spilling to disk under consistent load -- the workload is regularly asking for more than it's been given. Wasteful spend shows up as low utilization most of the time, always-on all-purpose clusters running idle overnight, or -- just as commonly -- a workload that's perfectly sized but running an inefficient query: a full table scan that proper partitioning, Z-ordering, or caching would shrink dramatically. That last case matters because it's easy to mistake for under-provisioning -- the job is slow, so the instinct is to scale up -- when the actual fix is cheaper and doesn't touch infrastructure at all. I'd always profile at the workload level (per-job DBU or Capacity Unit consumption, query plans) before resizing anything, because scaling up a wasteful workload just makes the waste more expensive.
questions.professionalAnswer:
My first move when a bill spikes faster than data volume is never to resize anything -- it's to profile. On Databricks, the structural fix I'd check first is whether production jobs are running on job clusters that tear down when done, or on all-purpose clusters that bill the whole time they're up, idle hours included -- that single mistake alone explains a lot of runaway bills. After that, autoscaling bounds, auto-termination, and cluster policies that cap what a team can spin up.

On Fabric, I'd pull up the Capacity Metrics app and actually look at utilization over time rather than guess at a SKU, and I'd lean on autoscale billing for genuine spikes instead of permanently sizing for peak load that only hits occasionally.

The real test for under-provisioned versus wasteful is what the utilization graph looks like, not what the bill looks like. Sustained high utilization, throttling, queued jobs -- that's genuinely under-provisioned, and scaling up is the right call. Low utilization most of the day, or an always-on cluster idling overnight -- that's wasteful. But there's a third case people miss: a perfectly-sized workload running a bad query, doing a full scan that partitioning or caching would fix -- that looks exactly like 'under-provisioned' if you only look at the bill, and scaling it up just makes the same inefficient query more expensive. So I always profile the workload first, before I touch any infrastructure setting.
commonMistakes: Scaling up a Databricks cluster or Fabric capacity SKU as the first response, without profiling actual utilization
Running scheduled production jobs on always-on all-purpose clusters instead of job clusters
Guessing at Fabric SKU sizing instead of using the Fabric Capacity Metrics app to see real utilization and throttling
Assuming a higher bill automatically means under-provisioning rather than checking for inefficient queries or unnecessary jobs first
Not using autoscaling or autoscale billing options already available on both platforms before resizing statically
keyPoints: Use job clusters with autoscaling and auto-termination instead of always-on all-purpose clusters for production workloads
Enforce sizing centrally via Databricks cluster policies
Use the Fabric Capacity Metrics app to see real utilization and throttling over time before resizing a SKU
Genuine under-provisioning shows as sustained throttling/queuing/SLA misses; wasteful spend shows as low utilization or inefficient queries
Profile at the workload level before resizing either platform
Query/code optimization can fix a problem that looks like under-provisioning without touching infrastructure at all

Correct Fabric capacity cost-optimization levers
Clear, workable method for distinguishing under-provisioned from wasteful
Practical profiling/monitoring approach before resizing

questions.title: PII Controls Across Unity Catalog and Fabric When the Same Data Is Accessed From Both
questions.prompt: Design a PII-handling architecture spanning Unity Catalog row- and column-level security on the Databricks side and Fabric's own sensitivity and governance controls on the Fabric side, for a platform where the same underlying customer data is accessed from both.
questions.modelAnswer:
On the Databricks side, Unity Catalog gives you native row filters and column masks defined directly on the table -- a row filter is a SQL function that restricts which rows a caller can see based on their group membership or attributes, and a column mask similarly redacts or nulls a sensitive column's value for callers who lack a specific grant. Both are enforced centrally by Unity Catalog's governance layer, which means they apply the same way whether the query comes from a notebook, a SQL warehouse, or a BI tool -- the enforcement point is the catalog, not the client. Tagging sensitive columns with a consistent taxonomy (pii, sensitivity=high) on top of that gives you an auditable inventory of exactly where PII lives.

On the Fabric side, governance increasingly runs through Microsoft Purview integration for sensitivity labeling (e.g., 'Confidential -- PII') on items and columns, which drives information-protection behavior like restricting export or sharing of labeled content, combined with Fabric-native row-level and column-level security defined either in the Power BI semantic model (roles with DAX row filters) or, for a Warehouse, through T-SQL security predicates that mirror what Unity Catalog's row filters do on the Databricks side.

The part that actually matters architecturally is this: if the same Delta table is owned in Unity Catalog and reached from Fabric through a OneLake Shortcut (or the reverse), the row filters and column masks defined in Unity Catalog do not automatically carry over to the Fabric access path, and Fabric's RLS/OLS and sensitivity labels don't automatically protect the Databricks access path either -- each platform enforces its own security model at its own boundary, and neither can be assumed to cover the other's entry point without explicitly verifying the specific integration available at the time. The safe design is to define PII classification once, in a shared, consistent tagging taxonomy across both catalogs, and then enforce it natively and redundantly on each side -- UC row filters and column masks for the Databricks path, Purview labels plus Fabric-native RLS/OLS for the Fabric path -- rather than assuming a single point of enforcement protects every way the data can be queried. I'd also centralize the audit logs from both Unity Catalog and Fabric/Purview activity logging into one monitoring pipeline, so PII access is observable regardless of which platform actually served the query.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd explain this to the team as two separate enforcement points that happen to be looking at the same underlying data. On Databricks, Unity Catalog's row filters and column masks are defined once on the table and enforced centrally, so it doesn't matter if the query comes from a notebook or a BI tool -- the catalog is the enforcement layer. On Fabric, it's Purview sensitivity labels for classification and export controls, plus native row-level and column-level security in the semantic model or Warehouse.

The thing I'd be most careful to call out is that these two don't automatically protect each other. If the same table is shared from Databricks into Fabric through a OneLake Shortcut, Unity Catalog's row filters don't just follow it across that boundary -- and Fabric's RLS doesn't reach back to protect the Databricks side either. Each platform enforces its own rules at its own door, and assuming otherwise is exactly how a PII leak happens through the access path nobody thought to check.

So my actual design is: classify PII once, with a consistent tag taxonomy used on both sides, then enforce it twice -- UC row filters and column masks on the Databricks path, Purview labels plus Fabric's native RLS/OLS on the Fabric path -- deliberately redundant rather than relying on one side to cover the other. And I'd pull the audit logs from both platforms into one place, because if someone asks 'who accessed this customer's data,' I want one answer regardless of which engine actually ran the query.

Assuming Fabric sensitivity labels alone restrict query-level access rather than primarily driving classification and export/DLP behavior
Defining PII rules in only one platform and assuming that covers every access path
Not centralizing audit logs from both platforms to verify enforcement is actually consistent
Inconsistent tagging of the same PII column across the two catalogs, so classification itself disagrees between platforms
keyPoints: Unity Catalog row filters and column masks enforce PII protection centrally on the Databricks side regardless of client
Fabric relies on Purview sensitivity labels plus native RLS/OLS in semantic models or Warehouse security predicates
Security defined in one platform does not automatically propagate across a OneLake Shortcut or similar cross-platform access path
Enforce PII protection independently and redundantly in each engine rather than assuming shared enforcement
Maintain one consistent PII tagging/classification taxonomy and centralize audit logging across both platforms

Correct Fabric/Purview sensitivity labeling and native RLS/OLS mechanics
Correctly identifies that enforcement doesn't automatically cross the shortcut/access-path boundary
Proposes consistent tagging and centralized audit logging across platforms

questions.title: Catching Schema Drift When Kafka and Nightly Batch Both Land in the Same Table
questions.prompt: Design schema drift handling for a hybrid pipeline where a Kafka-sourced streaming feed and a nightly batch feed both land in the same Delta/Lakehouse table, and the upstream team sometimes adds or renames fields without notice. Walk through where you'd actually catch it, and what should happen automatically versus what should alert a human.
questions.modelAnswer:
Drift needs to be caught at each source's own ingestion boundary, before either one reaches the shared table -- not after they've already merged, because by then a breaking change from one source has already corrupted a table that the other source also depends on. On the streaming side, that means parsing the Kafka payload against an explicit, versioned schema rather than letting Spark infer it -- ideally backed by a schema registry with compatibility rules, so a breaking producer-side change is flagged as early as the registry itself, not discovered downstream. On the batch side, Auto Loader's schema tracking (or an explicit comparison of the incoming file's schema against the last known-good schema before the write) plays the same role for the nightly drop.

What happens automatically versus what alerts a human depends entirely on whether the change is additive or breaking. A new, nullable column appended to the source is safe to auto-merge -- Delta's own schema evolution (mergeSchema) handles this cleanly, and no existing reader breaks because of an extra optional column. A renamed column, a changed type, or a dropped column is a different category entirely: auto-merging those silently either drops historical continuity under the old name, nulls out a field downstream code is still reading, or breaks a type assumption somewhere -- none of which should happen without a human looking at it first. For those, the pipeline should fail closed for that source's batch (or route the offending records to a quarantine/dead-letter location) rather than writing them into the shared table, and fire an alert with the specific diff -- what changed, which source, which run -- to whoever owns that pipeline.

Because streaming and batch hit the shared table on different cadences, each source's schema validation has to be independent -- a breaking change in the nightly batch shouldn't halt the streaming ingestion, and vice versa, so one source's drift doesn't take the whole shared table's ingestion down with it. Longer-term, the actual fix is upstream: pushing for a documented data contract with the source team that specifies what kind of evolution is allowed (additive-only, with a deprecation window for anything else) turns this from a recurring fire drill into something the pipeline can simply assume won't happen without warning.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd catch this at each source separately, before it ever reaches the shared table -- because once a breaking change from one feed lands in that table, it's corrupted for the other feed too. For the Kafka side, that means parsing against an explicit schema, ideally through a schema registry with compatibility rules, instead of letting Spark just infer whatever shape shows up. For the nightly batch, Auto Loader's schema tracking does the equivalent job -- compare against the last known schema before writing.

What I'd let happen automatically is purely additive changes -- a new nullable column just gets merged in via Delta's schema evolution, no drama, because nothing that already reads the table breaks from an extra optional field. Anything else -- a rename, a type change, a dropped column -- I don't want auto-merged at all. That should fail that source's run, or route the bad records to a quarantine table, and page whoever owns that pipeline with exactly what changed.

And I'd keep the two sources' validation completely independent, because they land on different schedules -- a bad nightly batch shouldn't take down the streaming ingestion, and a bad streaming schema shouldn't block the nightly batch. Beyond the pipeline fix, the thing I'd actually push for with the upstream team is a real data contract -- additive changes allowed freely, anything else needs a heads-up and a deprecation window -- because the pipeline catching this reactively every time is a symptom, not the actual fix.
commonMistakes: Relying on schema inference instead of an explicit expected schema, so renamed or new fields get silently accepted or silently nulled
Blindly using Delta's mergeSchema for every change, including breaking renames, which silently adds a column while losing historical continuity under the old name
Validating schema only after the two sources have already merged, so one source's drift corrupts the shared table for both
Having no alerting path, so breaking schema changes are discovered only when a downstream dashboard or query breaks
Not pushing for an upstream data contract, leaving the team permanently reactive to the same kind of surprise
keyPoints: Validate schema explicitly at each source's own ingestion boundary, before it reaches the shared table
Additive, nullable changes can be auto-merged safely via Delta's schema evolution
Breaking changes (renames, type changes, drops) should fail or quarantine the run and alert a human, never auto-merge silently
Keep streaming and batch schema validation independent so one source's drift doesn't block the other
Push for an upstream data contract to reduce recurring, unannounced drift

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes additive (auto-handle) from breaking (alert) schema changes
Proposes validation at each source's own ingestion boundary before the merge point
Correct quarantine/dead-letter and alerting design
Mentions a data contract as the longer-term fix
Clarity

questions.title: Sharding a Ride-Sharing Platform's Real-Time Analytics at Hundreds of Thousands of Events a Minute
questions.prompt: Design the data architecture -- ingestion, partitioning/sharding, and serving layer -- for a ride-sharing company's real-time analytics platform at a scale of hundreds of thousands of trip events per minute. Walk through how you'd shard or partition the data and what tradeoffs that creates for queries that need to span multiple shards.
questions.modelAnswer:
For ingestion at this volume, events (location pings, trip state changes) flow through Kafka or Event Hubs partitioned by a key that actually matches the platform's query locality -- geographic region or driver ID, not trip_id, since trip_id has no locality benefit and would just scatter related events randomly. Partitioning by geo-cell or city keeps a given region's event sequence ordered within its partition, which matters for dispatch-adjacent processing, and lets partition count and consumer parallelism scale against real throughput needs rather than an arbitrary default.

For sharding/storage, geography is the natural sharding key for the same reason: the overwhelming majority of ride-sharing queries -- supply/demand matching, surge pricing, dispatch -- are geo-local, so sharding by city or region means most queries stay within one shard and each shard's compute and storage scale independently. The real tradeoff shows up for queries that cross shard boundaries -- a platform-wide 'total trips this hour across every city' query, or a trip that spans two regions -- which require a fan-out/scatter-gather across shards and a merge step, adding real latency and complexity that a single-shard query never pays. The mitigation is maintaining a separate, incrementally updated global rollup -- each shard's gold-layer city aggregates feeding a platform-wide summary table -- so cross-shard analytical queries hit a small pre-aggregated dataset instead of live scatter-gather across every operational shard. Skew is also a real concern here: a mega-city shard (New York, Tokyo) can dwarf a small-city shard, so I'd sub-partition within large shards (by geo-cell or H3 hex) to avoid one city becoming a bottleneck on its own, the same underlying problem as a noisy tenant in a multi-tenant system.

For the serving layer, I'd deliberately separate two different needs rather than forcing one store to do both: a low-latency 'current state' store (nearest-driver matching, live location) optimized for point lookups and recent data, and a separate analytical serving store (Delta Lake, partitioned by date and region, Z-ordered on commonly filtered columns like city_id) optimized for aggregation over time. Trying to serve both dispatch-grade operational latency and historical analytical aggregation from the same store forces compromises neither workload should have to make, and the cross-shard rollups used for dashboards can tolerate seconds-level eventual consistency, which the live dispatch path cannot -- a reasonable tradeoff to accept for query speed on the analytics side.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd key ingestion by something with real locality -- geo-region or driver, not trip_id, since trip_id scatters related events with no benefit. That keeps a region's event sequence ordered within its Kafka partition, which matters for anything downstream that cares about sequence.

For sharding, geography is the obvious key here because almost every query this platform runs -- matching supply and demand, surge pricing, dispatch -- is local to one city or region anyway, so most queries never leave their shard. The tradeoff I'd flag up front is the query that does cross shards -- a platform-wide total, or a trip spanning two regions -- that's a scatter-gather across shards, and it's slower and more complex than a normal query by nature. I'd handle that by keeping a separately maintained global rollup that each shard feeds incrementally, so the cross-shard dashboard query hits a small pre-aggregated table instead of fanning out live across every shard every time. I'd also expect a few mega-city shards to dwarf the small ones, so I'd sub-partition those by geo-cell to avoid one city becoming the bottleneck for the whole shard.

For serving, I wouldn't try to make one store do both jobs. Dispatch and nearest-driver matching need a low-latency operational store built for point lookups; the analytics dashboards need a Delta Lake-style store built for scanning and aggregating over time. I'd let the cross-shard analytical rollups be eventually consistent, seconds of staleness, because that's a fine tradeoff for query speed on the dashboard side -- it's just not a tradeoff I'd accept on the live dispatch path.
commonMistakes: Sharding or partitioning by trip_id, which has no locality benefit and scatters related events randomly
Not planning for cross-shard rollups, discovering at query time that global aggregates require slow live scatter-gather over every shard
Ignoring severe geographic skew (mega-cities) and ending up with one oversized, bottlenecked shard
Conflating the real-time dispatch/matching system's latency needs with the analytics dashboard's needs and trying to serve both from one store
Not pre-aggregating anything, forcing every analytical query to scan raw event-level data across all shards
keyPoints: Partition/shard by a geography- or entity-based key that matches real query locality, not a high-cardinality key with no locality like trip_id
Maintain pre-aggregated cross-shard rollups so global analytical queries avoid live scatter-gather over every shard
Handle skewed shards (mega-cities) with further sub-partitioning
Separate the low-latency operational/dispatch serving need from the analytical dashboard serving need with different stores
Accept eventual consistency and seconds-level staleness in analytics rollups as a reasonable tradeoff for query speed

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct ingestion/partitioning key design with sound locality reasoning
Correct sharding strategy and skew-handling approach
Correct cross-shard rollup and serving-layer design
Addresses latency/consistency tradeoffs clearly
Clarity

questions.title: When an Indexed View Is Worth the Write Cost
questions.prompt: Your reporting dashboard runs an aggregation query against Production.Product (grouped by subcategory, computing a row count and total list price) hundreds of times per minute during business hours, and the underlying table is only touched by a handful of transactions a day. A teammate suggests materializing this aggregation as an indexed view. Walk through the real requirements for making that work, what SQL Server does differently once it's in place, and the ongoing cost you're trading for speed. Would you recommend it here -- and would your answer change if the table instead took thousands of writes per second?
questions.modelAnswer:
A regular view is just stored SQL text -- it re-runs its underlying SELECT every time it's queried. An indexed view is the one case where that's not true: once you create a unique clustered index on the view, SQL Server physically materializes the computed result set on disk, and queries against the view (or, on Enterprise edition, queries against the base table that the optimizer recognizes as equivalent) can read that pre-computed data directly instead of re-aggregating Production.Product every time.

Getting there has real, non-negotiable requirements: the view must be created WITH SCHEMABINDING, which locks the underlying table's structure so SQL Server can guarantee the view stays consistent with it -- you can't ALTER a schemabound table's referenced columns without dropping dependent objects first. Aggregations must use COUNT_BIG(*), not COUNT(*). A number of T-SQL constructs are disallowed inside the view's definition (TOP, several non-deterministic or imprecise functions, certain outer join shapes). And on non-Enterprise editions, the optimizer won't automatically substitute the indexed view for an equivalent base-table query -- you need the NOEXPAND hint to force it.

The cost is real and ongoing: every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE against Production.Product now has to maintain the materialized aggregate too, on top of the base table write. For this scenario -- read-heavy by a wide margin, with only a dozen or so writes a day -- that tradeoff is clearly worth it: you're paying a trivial amount of extra write overhead a handful of times daily to make hundreds of reads per minute avoid re-aggregating the table from scratch. If the table instead took thousands of writes per second, I'd recommend against it: the indexed view's maintenance cost would be paid on every single one of those writes, compounding exactly where you can least afford it, and I'd look at a separate pre-aggregated reporting table refreshed on a schedule, or a different caching layer, instead.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The way I'd frame it for the team: a normal view is free to create because it doesn't store anything -- it's just a saved query. An indexed view is different, and the trigger for that difference is adding a unique clustered index to it; the moment you do, SQL Server actually materializes the result on disk. To even get there you need WITH SCHEMABINDING on the view, COUNT_BIG instead of COUNT, and you have to accept that the view's definition is now more restricted -- no TOP, limited function support. And if we're not on Enterprise, I'd flag that the optimizer won't use it automatically; we'd need NOEXPAND in the query, or it just does the full aggregation anyway and we got nothing for the extra complexity.

The real decision point for me is the read/write ratio. In this case we've got maybe a dozen writes a day against hundreds of reads a minute, so I'd absolutely recommend the indexed view -- we're trading a tiny bit of extra work on writes that barely happen for a big win on reads that happen constantly. But if someone told me this table was taking thousands of writes a second, I'd push back hard on the same idea, because now every one of those writes has to keep the materialized aggregate in sync, and that's exactly the kind of hidden cost that tanks throughput on a hot table. In that case I'd rather build a separate summary table refreshed on a schedule, or push the aggregation into a different layer entirely.
questions.example:
CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID,
       COUNT_BIG(*) AS ProductCount,
       SUM(ListPrice) AS TotalListPrice
FROM Production.Product
WHERE ProductSubcategoryID IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY ProductSubcategoryID;
GO

CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_vw_ProductPriceSummary
ON dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary (ProductSubcategoryID);
GO

-- On Standard edition, force the optimizer to use the materialized data:
SELECT ProductSubcategoryID, ProductCount, TotalListPrice
FROM dbo.vw_ProductPriceSummary WITH (NOEXPAND);
commonMistakes: Forgetting WITH SCHEMABINDING, which indexed views require
Using COUNT(*) instead of the required COUNT_BIG(*)
Assuming the optimizer auto-uses the indexed view outside Enterprise edition without NOEXPAND
Ignoring write amplification and recommending indexed views for high-write tables
Not accounting for how SCHEMABINDING restricts future ALTER TABLE changes to the base table
keyPoints: Unique clustered index is what actually materializes the view's data
WITH SCHEMABINDING and COUNT_BIG(*) are mandatory requirements
Non-Enterprise editions need the NOEXPAND hint to use the indexed view
Every write to the base table now also maintains the materialized aggregate
Worth it for read-heavy, low-write-ratio reporting aggregations
Not worth it for tables with very high write throughput

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the materialization mechanism and unique clustered index requirement
Names the real requirements (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, restrictions)
Explains the ongoing write-maintenance cost
Gives a correct, justified recommendation for the low-write scenario
Correctly reverses the recommendation for the high-write scenario with reasoning
Mentions NOEXPAND / edition behavior

questions.title: Designing a Reusable Custom Operator for a Recurring Vendor API Extraction
questions.prompt: Six different DAGs each extract data from a different endpoint of the same third-party vendor API (same auth, same pagination style, same rate limits), and each one currently has its own copy-pasted PythonOperator with slightly different retry/backoff logic that's already drifted out of sync. Design a reusable custom operator (or operator + hook pair) architecture that fixes this, and explain what you'd put in the Hook versus the Operator.
questions.modelAnswer:
Split responsibilities the way Airflow's own provider packages do. A VendorApiHook (subclassing BaseHook or HttpHook) owns the connection concerns: reading the shared auth from an Airflow Connection, handling pagination, and rate-limit backoff/retry at the HTTP-call level, exposing a simple method like get_records(endpoint, params) that returns already-paginated, already-authenticated results. A VendorApiExtractOperator (subclassing BaseOperator) owns the task-level concerns: which specific endpoint to call, what to do with the returned records, templated fields for date ranges via Jinja, and Airflow-level retry/on_failure behavior.

The six DAGs then each instantiate VendorApiExtractOperator(endpoint="...", ...) with a few lines of config instead of a bespoke PythonOperator, and a rate-limit or auth fix lands once in the Hook and benefits all six immediately instead of needing six separate PRs. Package this as a small internal Python package (or an airflow_plugins module) so it's versioned and independently testable, with unit tests specifically against the Hook's pagination/backoff logic, since that's the part that drifted and broke trust in the first place.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'd pull the connection-level stuff -- auth, pagination, rate-limit backoff -- into a Hook, and leave the task-level stuff -- which endpoint, what to do with the records, retries, templated date ranges -- in an Operator that uses that Hook. That's exactly the split Airflow's own provider packages use.

Once that split exists, each of the six DAGs just instantiates the operator with its own endpoint and a few config values, instead of six copy-pasted PythonOperators. And when the rate-limit logic needs a fix, it gets fixed once in the Hook and all six DAGs get the fix automatically instead of six separate PRs that might drift again. I'd package this separately so it's versioned and has its own tests, specifically around the Hook's retry/backoff behavior, since that's the part that's already drifted once.
commonMistakes: Putting HTTP/pagination/retry logic directly in the operator's execute() method instead of a separate Hook, re-coupling connection logic to task logic
Leaving auth/rate-limit handling duplicated across DAGs instead of centralizing it in one Hook
Not versioning the shared Hook/Operator as its own testable package, so fixes still have to be copy-pasted or manually synced
Skipping templated fields, forcing each DAG to hardcode date logic differently
Not writing tests for the Hook's retry/backoff logic specifically, the exact part that drifted and broke trust
keyPoints: Hook owns connection/auth/pagination/rate-limit concerns, reusable across any task
Operator owns task-specific config and Airflow-level behavior (retries, templated fields)
Centralizing shared logic in one Hook means a fix benefits all six DAGs at once
Package and version the Hook/Operator independently so it's testable on its own
This mirrors how Airflow's own provider packages are structured

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct separation of Hook (connection/pagination/rate-limit) vs. Operator (task config/behavior) responsibilities
Explains how centralization fixes the drift problem
Recommends packaging/versioning/testing the shared component
Clear overall explanation

questions.title: Designing Secure Credential Management After a Data Factory Security Audit
questions.prompt: A security audit of your Data Factory environment found linked services with embedded SQL authentication connection strings, including a hardcoded password on one, and a service principal holding Owner on the entire subscription used for Blob Storage access. Design the correct credential and access architecture.
questions.modelAnswer:
For the hardcoded SQL password, the fix is to move it into Azure Key Vault and have the linked service reference it through Key Vault integration rather than storing it in plaintext in the pipeline definition or in any ARM template - that alone makes the credential centrally managed, rotatable, and no longer visible anywhere in source control or deployment artifacts. For the Blob Storage access using an Owner-scoped service principal, I'd go further than just better-hiding that credential: I'd replace it entirely with Data Factory's system-assigned (or user-assigned) managed identity, which removes the need to store or rotate a credential for that connection at all, since Azure handles the identity's authentication behind the scenes.

Whichever identity or service principal remains in use, I'd scope its RBAC role down to exactly what it needs at the narrowest resource boundary that works - Storage Blob Data Contributor on the specific storage account or container it actually touches, never Owner at the subscription level, which is wildly disproportionate to what a pipeline's data-movement activity actually requires. For SQL access specifically, I'd prefer Azure AD authentication via the managed identity where the target is Azure SQL, or if the source is on-premises SQL Server, I'd make sure the self-hosted integration runtime's own service account is tightly scoped and that whatever credential remains in Key Vault has a defined rotation and expiry policy rather than being set-and-forgotten. I'd close this out by removing the subscription-level Owner service principal entirely once the replacement access is validated, adding diagnostic logging and alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes to catch future drift, and scheduling a recurring (e.g., quarterly) access review so this becomes an ongoing control rather than a one-time cleanup following an audit finding.
questions.professionalAnswer: For the hardcoded password, that's the easy part to fix - move it into Key Vault and have the linked service pull it from there, so it's never sitting in plaintext in a pipeline definition or an ARM template again. The Owner-on-the-whole-subscription service principal is the part I'd actually spend more time on, because just hiding that credential better in Key Vault doesn't fix the underlying problem - the access itself is wildly overscoped. I'd replace it with Data Factory's managed identity wherever possible, so there's no stored credential at all for that connection, and then scope whatever RBAC role it actually needs down to the specific storage account, not the entire subscription. For SQL, I'd lean on Azure AD authentication through that same managed identity if it's Azure SQL, and if it's still on-prem, I'd make sure the self-hosted IR's service account and whatever's left in Key Vault has an actual rotation schedule instead of being set once and forgotten. And I wouldn't call this done after one cleanup pass - I'd want diagnostic alerts on Key Vault access and linked-service changes, plus a recurring access review, so this doesn't quietly drift back to where it started.
commonMistakes: Moving the password into Key Vault without also addressing the separately serious issue of subscription-level Owner scope
Not considering managed identity as a way to eliminate stored credentials entirely rather than just hiding them better
Granting a 'safer-sounding' but still overly broad role instead of the specific minimal RBAC role actually needed
Not planning credential rotation or an ongoing access review, treating this as a one-time cleanup
Not addressing authentication specifically for the on-premises SQL Server side
keyPoints: Key Vault-backed linked services eliminate plaintext/embedded credentials
Managed identity eliminates stored credentials for Blob Storage access entirely where supported
Scope RBAC to least privilege at the specific resource level, never subscription-level Owner
Prefer Azure AD authentication for SQL where possible
Establish ongoing credential rotation and periodic access review, not a one-time fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly proposes Key Vault integration for remaining credentials
Proposes managed identity to eliminate stored credentials where possible
Correctly scopes RBAC to least privilege
Addresses ongoing rotation/review process
Clarity

questions.title: Resolving a Databricks-vs-Fabric Decision After Two Engineers Start Unauthorized Prototypes
questions.prompt: You're the senior data engineer on a team deciding between building a new analytics workload on Databricks versus Microsoft Fabric. Leadership wants a clear recommendation, but two strong engineers on your team each have a personal preference for a different one and have started quietly building prototypes in their preferred tool without authorization. How do you resolve this and land on and justify a real architecture decision?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer separates two problems that are tangled together: the process violation of unauthorized, parallel prototyping, and the actual architecture decision. The candidate should address the first privately and non-punitively with each engineer before any group discussion -- not to punish the initiative, but to reset the expectation that exploratory spikes get flagged and time-boxed so the team isn't making a decision under sunk-cost pressure from hours already invested in a preferred tool.

For the decision itself, the candidate should describe a structured evaluation against real requirements -- cost at expected scale, latency needs, the team's existing skill depth, integration with the current warehouse and Power BI estate, operational overhead, and migration/lock-in risk -- rather than letting it become a referendum on which engineer 'wins.' A strong move is having each engineer present the case FOR the other tool, which forces genuine engagement with tradeoffs instead of defending territory. The final recommendation to leadership should be framed around business requirements and risk, with the rejected option's real strengths acknowledged, and explicitly should not be driven by which prototype is further along, since that would reward going around the process.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Honestly, the first thing I'd do is pull both engineers aside separately, before we're anywhere near a group conversation about Databricks versus Fabric, because the thing I actually need to deal with first isn't the tech choice -- it's that two people started building during work hours on tools nobody signed off on. I'd keep it low-key but direct: I'm not upset about which tool you like, I'm concerned that we're about to make a decision under pressure from sunk hours instead of on the merits.

Then for the actual decision, I'd get the team together and build a real scorecard -- cost at the scale we actually expect, how it plugs into our existing Power BI and warehouse setup, what our team already knows how to operate, and what we're locked into if we're wrong. And I'd specifically flip the script and ask each engineer to argue for the OTHER tool for ten minutes, because that's usually when you find out whether someone actually understands the tradeoffs or just has a preference. Whatever I take to leadership, I want it to be obviously about the requirements, not about whose prototype has more hours in it -- because if the further-along prototype wins by default, I've just taught the team that going around the process is how you win architecture debates.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight into the technical debate without addressing the unauthorized parallel work first
Letting the decision be influenced by which prototype happens to be further along (sunk cost)
Publicly calling out one or both engineers in a group setting instead of addressing it privately
Treating the decision as a popularity contest between the two engineers rather than a requirements-driven evaluation
Presenting leadership with a personal preference dressed up as a technical recommendation instead of real tradeoff data
keyPoints: Separates the process issue (unauthorized prototyping) from the architecture decision itself
Addresses the process issue privately and constructively, not punitively or in public
Builds a requirements-based evaluation framework rather than deciding by preference or sunk cost
Uses a technique (like arguing the other side) to force genuine engagement over tribal preference
Delivers a recommendation to leadership grounded in business tradeoffs, not personal or team politics

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Separates and correctly handles the unauthorized-prototyping process issue
Builds a genuine requirements-based decision framework instead of deciding by preference
Avoids letting sunk cost or prototype progress unfairly drive the outcome
Handles both engineers respectfully without public blame or favoritism
Produces a clear, defensible recommendation framed for leadership

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Engineer After a Delta Lake Migration Breaks Downstream Dashboards
questions.prompt: A junior engineer you're mentoring led a Delta Lake migration from legacy Parquet tables that went badly -- a schema mismatch caused several downstream dashboards to show wrong numbers for two days before anyone noticed. The junior engineer is visibly shaken and defensive. How do you handle this as their mentor, both in the moment and in the following weeks?
questions.modelAnswer:
In the moment, the priority is stabilizing both the person and the incident, in that order of urgency for the conversation even though the technical fix may come first in parallel. The candidate should describe opening with something that lowers defensiveness rather than confirms it -- acknowledging the migration was a real, valuable piece of work and that a schema mismatch slipping through for two days is a gap in the team's detection, not purely a personal failure. Piling on a visibly shaken junior engineer in the moment only teaches them to hide problems next time.

The candidate should also describe not skipping the substance: walking through what actually happened together -- why the schema mismatch wasn't caught, whether there was a validation step that should have existed, why the two-day detection gap happened -- so the junior engineer leaves with real understanding, not just reassurance. In the following weeks, a strong mentor follows up concretely: pairs with them on adding schema validation/contract checks to the pipeline, has them present the root cause to the team themselves (framed as ownership, not punishment), and checks in privately on their confidence, since a bad first ownership experience can make a promising engineer overly risk-averse if it isn't addressed.
questions.professionalAnswer:
In that first conversation, I'm not leading with the mistake -- they already know it went wrong, and they're already defensive, so hammering on it just makes them shut down. I'd start with something like, 'the migration itself was solid work, and this kind of schema gap is exactly the kind of thing our review process should have caught -- let's figure out together why it didn't.' That's not me letting them off the hook, it's me making sure the conversation can actually go somewhere useful instead of just being about how bad they feel.

Then I do want to go through the real mechanics with them -- why the schema mismatch wasn't flagged, why it took two days for anyone to notice wrong numbers, whether a validation step would have caught it -- because I want them to actually understand it, not just apologize for it. In the weeks after, I'd have them pair with me on building the schema validation we were missing, and I'd ask them to present what happened to the team themselves, framed as 'here's what I found and fixed,' not as a confession. And I'd check in with them one-on-one a couple times after, because a bad first solo-ownership experience can quietly make someone gun-shy for a long time if nobody checks on how they're actually feeling about it.
questions.example: Opening line: 'The migration itself was good work -- this gap is on our review process as much as anything. Let's walk through what happened together.'
commonMistakes: Leading with the failure/root cause before addressing the junior engineer's emotional state
Treating it purely as a one-on-one coaching moment and skipping a real technical root-cause walkthrough
Publicly framing the incident around the junior engineer's name instead of the systemic gap
Not following up in the following weeks, leaving the lesson and the confidence hit unresolved
Taking over the fix entirely instead of involving the junior engineer in building the actual remediation
keyPoints: Opens the in-the-moment conversation in a way that lowers defensiveness rather than confirms blame
Still walks through the real technical root cause so the lesson actually lands
Identifies and addresses the systemic detection gap (two days unnoticed), not just the schema mismatch
Involves the junior engineer in building the fix rather than fixing it for them
Follows up over subsequent weeks on both the technical skill and the engineer's confidence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Handles the junior engineer's emotional state constructively without skipping accountability
Conducts a genuine technical root-cause walkthrough with the engineer
Identifies the systemic detection gap as a separate issue from the schema mismatch itself
Involves the junior engineer in building the remediation rather than doing it for them
Describes concrete follow-up over the following weeks, not just the initial conversation

questions.title: Owning a Production Databricks Failure You Personally Caused With a Config Change
questions.prompt: You're the engineer of record when a production Databricks pipeline feeding an executive-facing report fails at 2 AM and isn't caught until a VP notices stale numbers at 8 AM. You personally made a config change to that pipeline two days earlier. How do you own this incident -- immediate response, communication, and the postmortem?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the six-hour detection gap as being at least as important as the failure itself, and treats personal ownership as something to state plainly and early rather than something to be drawn out. Immediately on learning of the failure, the candidate should describe triaging and fixing the pipeline first, then proactively communicating -- not waiting to be asked -- to the VP and relevant stakeholders with a clear, factual status: what broke, what's being done, a realistic ETA for backfilled/corrected numbers, and an acknowledgment that it traces to a config change made two days earlier.

The candidate should explicitly avoid two failure modes: minimizing their own role ('it was a config issue' without naming who made it) and over-apologizing in a way that derails the message stakeholders actually need (the fix and timeline). In the postmortem, the candidate should drive two separate findings: why the specific config change caused the failure and what validation should have caught it before deploy, and why the pipeline's monitoring/alerting didn't surface the failure for six hours, which is arguably the more important long-term fix since it's what turned a bug into a VP-visible incident. They should leave with named, dated action items -- alerting on this pipeline's freshness/SLA, a pre-deploy validation or canary step -- and should volunteer to drive those fixes themselves.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The second I know about it, my focus splits into two tracks at once: get the pipeline fixed and the numbers corrected, and get ahead of the communication instead of waiting for someone to come find me. I'd reach out to the VP and whoever else needs it directly -- here's what broke, here's that it traces back to a config change I made two days ago, here's what I'm doing about it, here's when the numbers will be right. I'm not going to bury that it was my change, but I'm also not going to spend the message apologizing instead of giving people the information they actually need right now.

In the postmortem, I actually want to push the conversation toward something bigger than 'my config change broke it' -- yes, we need to understand exactly why that change caused the failure and what pre-deploy check would've caught it, but the thing that actually turned this into a VP noticing stale numbers at 8 AM is that nothing paged anyone for six hours. That's the gap I care more about fixing long-term. I'd come out of that meeting with real, dated action items -- freshness alerting on this pipeline, some kind of canary check before this class of config change ships -- and I'd volunteer to own building them myself, since it's my mistake that surfaced the gap.
commonMistakes: Waiting for the VP or stakeholders to discover and raise the issue instead of communicating proactively
Being vague about personal ownership of the config change that caused the failure
Over-apologizing to the point that the actual fix and timeline get lost in the message
Treating the postmortem as only about the config change and ignoring the six-hour detection/alerting gap
Not following through with concrete, dated action items after the postmortem conversation ends
keyPoints: Fixes the immediate pipeline issue while proactively communicating status, not waiting to be asked
States personal ownership of the config change plainly, without minimizing or over-apologizing
Separates the root cause of the failure from the separate failure of detection/alerting taking six hours
Drives the postmortem toward concrete, dated action items rather than just a narrative
Volunteers to own the follow-up fixes rather than leaving them unassigned

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Prioritizes fixing the pipeline and proactive stakeholder communication immediately
Owns the config change plainly without minimizing or over-apologizing
Identifies the detection/alerting gap as a distinct, equally important finding
Produces concrete, owned, dated postmortem action items
Maintains clear, factual, non-defensive communication throughout

questions.title: Moving a Portal-Clicking Team to Terraform/Bicep Over Skeptical Senior Pushback
questions.prompt: Your team has always provisioned Azure resources by clicking through the portal, and you want to move the team to Terraform/Bicep for a new data platform build. Two senior teammates are skeptical, citing 'it's slower than just clicking the thing I need' and past frustration with a previous team's over-engineered Terraform setup. How do you negotiate this adoption?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats the skepticism as legitimate signal rather than resistance to be overcome by mandate. The candidate should start by separating the two objections, since they need different responses: 'portal is faster for a one-off' is often true and should be acknowledged honestly rather than argued away, while the past bad experience with over-engineered Terraform is a real scar that a new rollout needs to explicitly design against -- by keeping the initial module set small, flat, and genuinely necessary rather than building abstraction layers nobody asked for.

The candidate should propose an approach that lets the skeptics experience the value rather than being told about it: start with a new, lower-stakes piece of the platform build, let the team keep clicking for genuinely one-off exploratory resources for now, and bring the skeptics into writing the first modules rather than handing them a framework decided in isolation. The real argument for adoption -- consistent, reviewable, repeatable environments; drift detection; faster disaster recovery -- should be made concretely against this specific platform build's needs, not as an abstract best-practice argument, and the candidate should be honest that there's a real short-term velocity cost that pays off over the project's lifetime, not instantly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't go in trying to win an argument -- I'd go in treating their pushback as two separate, legitimate points that need different answers. 'Clicking is faster for the thing I need right now' is just true a lot of the time, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But 'the last Terraform setup I used was over-engineered and painful' is the one I actually need to address head-on, by being explicit that whatever we build this time starts small and flat -- no module-of-modules, no abstraction for things we don't have yet.

Practically, I'd rather let them feel the benefit than argue them into it. I'd pick a lower-stakes piece of the new platform build to go first, keep it genuinely simple, and actually have the two of them help write those first modules instead of handing them something I designed alone and asking them to adopt it. questions.title: Keeping a Kafka-vs-Fabric-Eventstreams Design Disagreement From Turning Personal
questions.prompt: You and a peer engineer disagree, in a design review, about whether a new real-time feature should be built on Kafka (which your company already runs) or Fabric Eventstreams (which the new Fabric-based analytics platform natively supports). The disagreement is starting to feel personal between the two of you. How do you navigate this disagreement productively in front of the rest of the team?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer recognizes the moment the disagreement tips from technical to personal and acts on it in real time rather than pushing through the meeting and letting it fester. The candidate should describe naming it lightly and without accusation -- something like suggesting they take the specific sub-disagreement offline, or proposing a short pause -- rather than continuing to escalate the exchange in front of the team, which erodes both their credibility and the team's trust in the review process.

Substantively, the candidate should refocus both of them on the actual decision criteria rather than who is 'right': operational cost of running two streaming systems versus consolidating onto one, the team's existing Kafka operational maturity versus the native integration benefits of Eventstreams within the new Fabric platform, and the specific feature's latency/throughput needs. A strong answer also addresses repairing the relationship afterward -- a brief one-on-one check-in with the peer after the meeting to make sure the disagreement doesn't linger as a grudge -- since unresolved peer friction tends to resurface in the next design review if it isn't addressed directly.
questions.professionalAnswer:
The moment I notice it's stopped being about Kafka versus Eventstreams and started being about the two of us, I want to call that out myself, gently, rather than keep going until someone else has to referee it. Something like, 'I think we're both dug in here more than this specific point deserves -- can we park this exact sub-question and come back to it with data?' That's not me conceding the technical point, it's me protecting the meeting and honestly protecting the two of us from saying something we'll regret in front of the team.

Then I'd try to drag us both back to what actually matters for the decision -- what does it cost us operationally to run two streaming systems instead of consolidating, how mature is our Kafka operations versus what we'd get for free with Eventstreams inside the new Fabric platform, and what does this specific feature actually need in terms of latency. And afterward, I'd go find him separately, just to check we're good -- because if I let that kind of friction sit unaddressed, it's going to show up again in the next design review, probably worse.

Winning the point in the room but leaving the relationship unresolved afterward

Avoiding the topic afterward out of discomfort, letting it resurface in a future meeting

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Three-Week Fabric Rollout Deadline Set Without Engineering Input
questions.prompt: Leadership wants a new multi-region Fabric capacity rollout finished in three weeks, driven by a sales commitment made without engineering input. Your honest estimate, based on capacity planning and testing, is six weeks. How do you push back on this deadline?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer pushes back with specifics and options rather than a flat refusal or a quiet, resentful compliance. The candidate should describe bringing the estimate's basis, not just the number -- what the capacity planning and testing actually showed, which steps take the time (region failover validation, capacity unit sizing under real load, security/governance configuration per region), and why compressing them risks a worse outcome than being two weeks late: a rushed multi-region rollout that fails under real load is more damaging to the sales relationship than a later, working one.

Rather than presenting a binary six-versus-three, the candidate should bring options: a phased rollout where the highest-priority region goes live first within a tighter timeframe while the rest follow on the original six-week plan, or a reduced-scope three-week version with explicitly named risks and gaps the business can choose to accept. The candidate should also address the process gap directly but diplomatically -- requesting that engineering get a seat at the table before future sales commitments involving infrastructure timelines are made, since this is likely to recur otherwise.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I'm not going to just say 'six weeks, take it or leave it' and I'm also not going to quietly try to cram six weeks of real work into three and hope it holds together. I'd bring the actual basis for the estimate -- here's what the capacity testing showed, here's specifically what eats the time, region failover validation, sizing capacity units under real load, per-region governance config -- so it's not just my gut feeling versus a sales number.

Then I'd come with options instead of just a rejection. Maybe we can get the highest-priority region live in three weeks and phase the rest in over the following weeks on the original plan, or if they really need all regions in three weeks, I'll tell them exactly what we'd be cutting and the risk that comes with it, and let the business decide if that tradeoff is worth it. And separately, I do want to raise -- carefully, not as a complaint -- that we need engineering in the room before commitments like this get made to customers, because otherwise we're going to keep having this exact conversation.

Framing the pushback as personal frustration rather than a risk-based business tradeoff

questions.title: Explaining a Fabric Capacity Cost Overrun to an Upset, Non-Technical VP of Finance
questions.prompt: A Fabric capacity you're responsible for had a cost overrun last month -- nearly double the budgeted spend -- because of an unbounded Dataflow Gen2 refresh schedule nobody caught in review. You have to explain this to a non-technical VP of Finance who is understandably upset. How do you handle that conversation?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer leads with plain acknowledgment and a non-technical explanation before moving into prevention, since a VP of Finance in this moment needs to know three things in order: what happened in terms they can act on, that it's already contained, and that it won't recur. The candidate should avoid jargon-heavy explanations ('an unbounded Dataflow Gen2 refresh schedule') and instead translate: a process that updates data kept re-running far more often than it needed to, consuming far more capacity than budgeted, and it wasn't caught because the team didn't yet have a cost-review step for this kind of change.

The candidate should take direct ownership of the review gap without being defensive or over-apologizing at length, since the VP needs confidence restored more than remorse performed. The answer should include concrete prevention: budget alerts/thresholds on Fabric capacity spend going forward, a required cost-impact check for refresh schedule changes before they ship, and a commitment to report back with the fix in place within a specific timeframe. A strong candidate also proactively addresses whether a credit or adjustment is possible, since the VP's immediate concern is the budget impact, not just the technical story.
questions.professionalAnswer:
With a VP of Finance, I'm not going to walk in and start explaining Dataflow Gen2 refresh internals -- I'd translate it immediately: a process that refreshes our data was running far more often than it needed to, and because we didn't have a cost check in place for that kind of change, it ran up nearly double our usual spend before anyone caught it. I'd say that plainly and not bury it in qualifiers.

Then I want to move fast into 'here's what's already fixed and here's what stops this happening again' -- I'd have capacity spend alerts in place going forward, and a required check on cost impact before we ship a refresh schedule change, and I'd give them a specific date I'll confirm those are live. And I'd ask directly whether there's anything we can do about the overrun itself, because I know the budget hit is the actual thing they're upset about, not the technical story behind it -- and I'd rather own that head-on than spend the meeting explaining myself.

questions.title: Leading a Blameless Postmortem on a Terraform Apply That Took Down a Shared Event Hub
questions.prompt: A `terraform apply` run by a teammate, approved in a rushed review, took down a shared production Event Hub namespace for 40 minutes before anyone noticed. You're leading the blameless postmortem. How do you run it so it's genuinely blameless but still produces real accountability and fixes?
questions.modelAnswer:
Blameless does not mean avoiding naming what happened -- the postmortem should state plainly that a specific Terraform change, approved in a rushed review, triggered the outage, while keeping the framing on the system that allowed it rather than on the individuals as people. The candidate should reframe the central question from 'who broke the Event Hub' to 'what let a plan with this blast radius get approved in a rushed review, and why did it take 40 minutes to notice a shared production namespace was down.' That reframing is what produces durable fixes instead of two people -- the author and the reviewer -- feeling punished while the same gap exists for the next risky change.

The candidate should explicitly involve both the author and the reviewer in walking through their reasoning: what the plan output looked like, what time pressure existed, why the blast radius of the change (a shared resource used by other teams) wasn't flagged in review. The postmortem should close with concrete, owned, dated action items distinct from the individuals' behavior -- for example, requiring plan output to explicitly call out changes to shared/cross-team resources, a mandatory second reviewer or cooling-off period for changes touching shared infrastructure, and alerting on the Event Hub namespace's health so a future outage is caught in minutes, not 40.
questions.professionalAnswer:
Blameless doesn't mean we're vague about what happened -- I'll say directly that a specific apply, approved in a review that got rushed, is what took the namespace down. But I keep steering the room toward the system question: what let a change with this big a blast radius get approved quickly, and why did it take 40 minutes before anyone noticed a shared production resource was gone, rather than who personally messed up.

I'd ask both the person who wrote the change and the person who reviewed it to actually walk through their side -- what the plan output showed, what the time pressure looked like, whether anything flagged that this touched a resource other teams depend on. And I'm not going to let the meeting end as just a good conversation -- I want it to end with specific fixes: plan output that calls out changes to shared resources explicitly, maybe a required second reviewer or a short cooling-off window for anything touching shared infra, and health alerting on that namespace so next time we catch it in minutes instead of 40.

Focusing on the individual author's or reviewer's judgment instead of the systemic review gap
Not inviting both the author and the reviewer to explain their actual context and reasoning
Treating the 40-minute detection delay as a footnote instead of an equally important separate finding
Ending with a narrative discussion but no concrete, owned, dated action items

questions.title: Building Buy-In for Unity Catalog Governance Against 'This Is Just Red Tape' Pushback
questions.prompt: You want to move your organization from ad hoc, tribal-knowledge-based data access (people just asking in Slack for someone to grant them access) to formal Unity Catalog-based governance with defined roles and approval workflows. Several senior stakeholders see this as unnecessary red tape that will slow them down. How do you build buy-in?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer treats 'this will slow us down' as a legitimate concern to design against, not an objection to argue past. The candidate should start by making the current cost of the ad hoc system visible and concrete rather than arguing governance in the abstract -- for example, surfacing real incidents or near-misses this org has already had: someone retaining access to sensitive tables long after they changed teams, a data incident where nobody could quickly answer who had access to what, or the compliance/audit burden of answering 'who can see this data' with no system of record.

The candidate should then design the rollout to actually address the speed concern rather than dismiss it: pre-approved role templates for common access patterns so routine requests are fast, a clear SLA for approval turnaround, and starting with the highest-sensitivity data first rather than a blanket policy that slows down everything at once. Involving the skeptical senior stakeholders in defining the role templates themselves turns them from objectors into co-owners. The candidate should also be honest that some friction is an intentional tradeoff for auditability and security, not a flaw to apologize for, while committing to measuring and tuning the approval SLA so it doesn't become the thing people feared.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I wouldn't try to win this by arguing governance is good in the abstract -- that's a losing argument against 'but it'll slow me down.' I'd rather make the actual cost of what we do today visible: did we have someone keep access to sensitive tables for months after switching teams, could we answer quickly who had access to what the last time something came up. If those stories exist in this org, that's a much stronger case than any governance slide.

Then I'd design the rollout specifically to answer the speed objection instead of brushing it off -- pre-approved templates for the common, routine access patterns so most requests are basically instant, a real SLA on anything that needs approval, and starting with the most sensitive data instead of slowing down everything on day one. And I'd actually bring the skeptical senior folks into defining those templates with me, because once they've helped build it, they're not objecting to someone else's red tape anymore, they're defending their own design. I would be upfront, though, that some friction is the point for the genuinely sensitive stuff -- that's not a bug I'm apologizing for, it's the tradeoff we're making on purpose.

questions.title: Resolving an Exactly-Once vs. At-Least-Once Disagreement on a Billing Pipeline
questions.prompt: You and a teammate disagree about whether a new client-facing billing pipeline needs true exactly-once processing (more complex, more expensive to build and run) or whether at-least-once with idempotent downstream writes is good enough. The teammate thinks you're over-engineering; you think they're underestimating the cost of a double-billed customer. How do you resolve this technical disagreement in a way that actually lands on the right answer for the business?
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong answer avoids resolving this as a purely technical argument about processing semantics and instead reframes it as a business-risk question that the business, not the two engineers, should ultimately help weigh. The candidate should note a key technical point: at-least-once delivery with properly designed idempotent downstream writes (deduplication keys, idempotency tokens on the write) can in practice achieve the same outcome as exactly-once for this use case, at lower complexity and cost -- so the real question isn't 'exactly-once vs. at-least-once' in the abstract, it's whether the team can actually guarantee idempotency correctly on every downstream write path, including retries and partial failures.

The candidate should describe proposing a concrete test of that assumption -- a review of every downstream write path for true idempotency guarantees, plus fault-injection testing that simulates duplicate and out-of-order delivery -- rather than either side asserting their position. If idempotency can be proven solid, at-least-once is the right, cheaper choice; if any write path can't be made cleanly idempotent, that's concrete evidence for the added complexity, not just a feeling. The candidate should also note that for a billing pipeline specifically, the cost of being wrong (double-billing a customer, reputational and refund cost) should explicitly be weighed against the cost of building and maintaining the more complex system, ideally with input from someone who owns that business risk.
questions.professionalAnswer:
I don't think this gets resolved by one of us convincing the other -- I'd rather turn it into something we can actually test. The real technical point is that at-least-once with genuinely idempotent downstream writes can behave just like exactly-once for this use case, so the actual question isn't the abstract semantics, it's whether we can really guarantee idempotency on every write path, including retries and partial failures, not just the happy path.

So I'd propose we go audit every downstream write together and run some fault-injection tests that throw duplicate and out-of-order events at it. If idempotency holds up cleanly everywhere, I'm fine admitting at-least-once is the right call and I was overweighting the risk. If even one write path can't be made properly idempotent, that's real evidence for the complexity, not just my gut feeling about double-billing being bad. And either way, for something billing-related, I think the cost of getting this wrong versus the cost of building the more complex system is a business tradeoff, not just an engineering preference -- so I'd want whoever owns that risk in the room for the final call, not just the two of us.

Not involving someone who owns the actual business risk (billing error cost) in the final decision
